Our results indicate that extending Emergency Department stays by 30 minutes may not be beneficial for most patients, but could be advantageous for certain high-risk patients who require prolonged treatment.

This study investigates how a group of agents resolves a shared decision-and-q learning problem where each agent must navigate a complex environment with hidden state conditions, receive reward or penalty signs, and share a reward-sharing network (RSN). The RSN is structured such that the difficulty of each task is encoded in a parameter that affects all agents, or is distributed among multiple parameters, affecting specific groups or individual agents. The latter scenario represents a distributed RSN (DRSN). Our findings show that the distribution of task difficulties influences the decision-making strategies of the agents, and using local information alone leads to suboptimal results, although sharing reward signs and using the RSN yields better outcomes. The suboptimal nature of local-based policies becomes more pronounced with increased difficulty distributions. Additionally, our analysis reveals that, although initial performance differences between groups exist, especially those with extreme difficulty distributions, these performance gaps disappear over time, and groups tend to converge on similar policies. Furthermore, our results indicate the potential for groups to surpass individual capabilities, and effective use of the RSN results in the greatest benefits when difficulty distribution is extremely high.

We investigated how background effects related to local charge conservation impact the measurement of charge-dependent correlations in nuclear collisions. Utilizing a simplified event structure, we derived an analytical formula for calculating the correlation coefficient and examined how events with either single- or multi-charge clusters are arranged in a quark-gluon plasma. We found that the correlation coefficient under the soft collective flow scenario depends on the interaction cross-section and is sensitive to whether a cluster consists of an odd or even number of charges. Additionally, our results suggest that the correlation structure observed in heavy-ion collisions can be reproduced by other mechanisms, such as long-range flow and initial conditions. Therefore, the measurement of the correlation structure cannot strictly verify or validate any single theoretical model. Nonetheless, the correlation measurement can critically assess the reliability of various physical models in describing the experimentally measured correlation structure.

This study provides a comprehensive examination of cultural and
economical implications of crowdfunding, offering an in-depth analysis at
three distinct levels: project details, project implementation, and crowd
behavior. Our research delves into predictive topics such as predicting the
likelihood of project success or calculating revenue potential. Additionally,
we explored non-deterministic aspects of crowdfunding, such as how different
types of cultural content produced more funds than projects with a technical
orientation. Our findings were derived from a combined dataset of GitHub and
Kickstarter, which provided a rare opportunity to study crowdfunded projects
side-by-side with other development projects. By doing so, we were able to
relate crowdfunding levels to the quality of programmers involved and
establish a quantitative connection with established software development
principles.

A novel federated learning framework, IL2, aims to address several key issues in machine learning that relate to privacy and collaboration. IL2 facilitates the cooperative development of intrusion detection systems by multiple organizations, while ensuring the confidentiality of each organization's data. This is achieved through IL2's decentralized approach to training a machine learning model, where federal nodes collect local models, combine them to form a unified one, and distribute it back to the participating organizations. Notably, a significant benefit of IL2 is the ability to control the degree of data sharing on a per-sample basis, allowing organizations to protect their most sensitive information. Our work includes the design of IL2, as well as an in-depth evaluation of its performance, running on a real-world intrusion detection dataset with actual code, stored in a live code repository.

Online motion planning for robots has generally focused on planning in the absence of feedback from the environment. However, advanced robotic systems can now gather real-world feedback. All existing real-world feedback task planning algorithms are either limited to single-shot solutions or maintain a constant computational load, regardless of the availability of feedback. Our research introduces an algorithm designed to take advantage of environmental feedback, resulting in significantly faster task execution and improved efficiency. The new algorithm is based on an incremental planning method that gradually updates the environment map and optimizes the trajectory, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation tests.

This study investigates the performance of gate materials using cutting-edge transmission line method to examine gate leakage current in high-mobility semiconductor devices. We compared three gate materials - gate electrode and gate dielectric - made of different metals, specifically aluminum, tungsten, and a low-workfunction gate, and measured their effect on gate voltage, frequency, and mobility in a 300mm semiconductor process. Our results indicate that the choice of gate material is instrumental in improving the mobility of semiconductor devices. By using optimized gate materials, we were able to achieve a maximum mobility of 176.8% and observe threshold voltage reduction of up to 91% with a frequency range of 100kHz to 5MHz. We also found that variation in gate length and orientation has a more significant impact on gate mobility at higher frequencies. Our study further reveals that the type of gate dielectric used has a limited effect on gate mobility in comparison to the choice of gate material.

We studied how a distributed oscillator system, consisting of identical oscillators with a unique frequency, behaves under various external influences. When we applied a distributed frequency deviation to the oscillators, the system became synchronized in multiple cycles, regardless of the complexity of its network structure. This robust group synchronization remained stable as long as a specific condition was met: the cumulative effect of its individual parts must be greater than the largest possible interaction between two components. To evaluate the influence of minor system variations, we applied a combination of mathematical and numerical methods, utilizing both traditional and innovative approaches. Our findings provide valuable insights for controlling and managing complex distributed oscillator systems.

Our study involves a timely topic, given the recent blockage of Google and its implications for global information access. With Google now blocked in major parts of India, we examine how other search engines like Bing and Yahoo handle domain blocking. Notably, our research reveals an intriguing instance where Bing and Yahoo seemingly bypass YouTube's domain block by listing alternative domains, yet fail to do the same for other blocked domains. Additionally, all three search engines appear to consistently exclude additional popular video hosting platforms beyond YouTube. This unique phenomenon raises questions about the reasons behind these patterns and their potential connections to the power dynamics at play between dominant online platforms like Google, YouTube, and the Indian government.

We've developed an approach to apply the $\beta$-function methodology in scenarios with broad monodromy defects, building on previous work without defects in [1,2]. In this case, we're considering a system of two pre-accelerated $Usp(4)$ gauge fields coupled with a single Dirac fermion, undergoing a 't Hooft anomaly with $U(1)_L \times U(1)_R$ as gauge symmetry. The presence of monodromy defects is characterized by an integer topological invariant derived from the 't Hooft loop. This leads to the introduction of a effective coupling, $\bar{\beta}$, that adheres to an nonlinear differential equation, striking similarities with systems without defects. However, the slope of $\bar{\beta}$ differs from its defect-free counterpart. Furthermore, we found that upon increasing the charge of the monodromy defect, the system transitions through a phase where it mimics the behavior of a system without defects. Additionally, we have found that for certain values of the pre-acceleration, the system exhibits a phase where the pre-acceleration effective coupling shows a linear increase. In both cases, this behavior is fully consistent with the established literature.

Over finite fields, we develop simplified expressions for the number of $K$-rational points of order $13$ on elliptic curves defined over cubic Galois extensions with absolute Galois group $S_{4,13}$. Similarly, we formulaically represent the count of $K$-rational points on elliptic curves over these extensions, given the presence of a point with order $13$. This order reflects the characteristics of its defining field, which has specific properties under the absolute Galois group $S_{4,13}$.

We investigate the fundamental characteristics of one-dimensional GANT and PH networks, focusing on the medium and high local delay regimes. The study reveals that these systems exhibit unique behaviors, distinct from the previously analyzed low local delay regime. In particular, it is found that one-dimensional GANT and PH networks with medium local delays on 'X/Y' nodes and 'Z/W' edges, where X/Y represents a distribution with finite mean and variance, and Z/W represents a standard exponential distribution, behave differently from their low local delay counterparts. Additionally, it is demonstrated that one-dimensional GANT and PH networks, characterized by arbitrary delay distributions on 'X/Y' nodes and 'Z/W' edges, and a finite mean on 'Z/W' edges, are uniquely shaped by their distribution functions under medium local delays. Furthermore, it is established that one-dimensional GANT and PH networks, distinguished by distinct delay distributions on 'X/Y' nodes and 'Z/W' edges, and a finite mean on 'Z/W' edges, are distinguishable within a high local delay regime.

Semi-supervised node classification in Graph Neural Networks using few labeled nodes and many unlabeled nodes has seen significant advancements, with a rise in pseudo-labeling techniques contributing substantially to their success. Despite pseudo-labeling's widespread use, it has not been rigorously examined how it influences GNNs' internal representations. Consequently, there is limited understanding of how choosing a GNN architecture, a learning method, and a pseudo-labeling strategy affects the resulting representations. Furthermore, most existing pseudo-labeling approaches have been assumed to enhance accuracy, but we aim to provide insights into their potential limitations. Through our analysis, we observed that using pseudo-labeling with certain GNN architectures and learning methods can limit performance, emphasizing the need to optimize model selection. Our findings suggest that a label propagation-based pseudo-labeling method may condition GNN representations, potentially leading to overconfidence in inaccurate predictions. To mitigate this, we employed a simple ensemble technique, combining models with and without pseudo-labeling, which yielded consistent results across four evaluated GNN architectures and four real-world datasets. Our study's implications suggest that pseudo-labeling, rather than improving node classification, may actually alter the resulting GNN representations.

Our research introduces PatchNet, a lightweight convolutional neural network specifically designed for processing video footage. Unlike conventional approaches using 3D convolution methods, PatchNet employs an innovative strategy where 2D sliding windows with a height of one pixel are convolved with corresponding features in each frame. This novel approach enables efficient and accurate temporal feature extraction for the subsequent fusion process. The fused channels, obtained through simple fusion of corresponding features in each frame, are then used to develop multiple downsample paths similar to MobileNetV2, resulting in multiple output layers. These layers are combined and used as the base feature extractor, followed by a classification head for the final predictions. Our model is comprised of efficient, easily interpretable, and adaptable statistical logic operations, making it highly suitable for object detection tasks in video footage. Our experiments are multi-faceted: we first evaluate our model across various video object detection tasks and metrics and found it to be comparable to state-of-the-art approaches. We then conducted an ablation study to demonstrate the effectiveness of each component and found that our model performs better than MobileNetV2 on these tasks. Lastly, our analysis of computational efficiency reveals that our model offers better latency and throughput than MobileNetV2, making it a more efficient and accurate design.

We analyze multi-point distribution in a discrete time TASEP with arbitrary initial conditions, specifically obtaining an exact closed-form formula for any number of observation times. This formalism enables subsequent calculation of moments via a straightforward application of the observed formula. We particularly examine the case of multiple distribution evaluations at a single observation time, solving an associated inverse problem in a related context.

This study assesses the energy efficiency of multi-user Multiple-Input Single-Output networks that use Switched Beam and SWIPT, with an optimization problem solved using a Tuning Method and Fractional Programming techniques, yielding an algebraic solution and simulated results.

This paper develops a perturbation theory for SU(N) fermions using an approach applied to QCD in a previous study and contrasts it with second-order renormalization techniques. We explore the perturbation series expansion of the SU(N) Yang-Mills coupling constant, $\alpha_s$, by examining the self-energy and vertex corrections at successive orders. Notably, these predictions lack the precision of corresponding second-order outcomes but hold potential for further mathematical simplification.

In the standard quantum treatment of optomechanics, the quantum description is essential only in limited areas of the beam's phase space. A general method is developed to map the full phase space of a quantum optical system into its classical representation. The method is applied to an electric circuit model analog, which is then used to experimentally investigate the quantum-backreaction force in large-occupation-number regimes. The method and the derived classical equations are validated through simulations of a simple optomechanical system, which also highlight the importance of quantum corrections in accurately describing the classical dynamics.

On the nonnegative axis, a continuous linear operator $\mathfrak{L}$ acts on the space $L^2(\mathbb{R}_{+}, \rho_{6g})$, where $\rho_{6g}$ represents a generalized sextic Freud weight function. This operator is closely related to a differential operator with a hyperbolic polynomial of degree six, enabling the introduction of six positive eigenvalues. Various characteristics of the operator, such as its essential spectrum, resolvent positivity, and approximate eigenvalues, are explored. Furthermore, a comparative study is made with the generalized Airy weight, and it is observed that the sextic Freud weight exhibits more robust properties.

A simple wall-following robot trajectory model is developed using a robot that follows a wall while keeping a certain distance from it. The robot's field of view and distance sensor's field of view are both considered in the study, which reveals that the robot's trajectory differs based on these factors. The theoretical findings are supported with simulated and real-world experiments using a mobile robot navigating along a straight wall. The study specifically looks at how the robot's field of view and distance sensor affect its movement, identifying previously overlooked factors such as the robot's height and sensor's angle of view.

This paper focuses on subalgebras of perturbative algebraic quantum field theory, using an approach based on geometric methods. We define a subalgebra in terms of a Cauchy surface and examine its structure, determining the relevant combinatorial objects and their symmetry properties. Our analysis reveals that the choice of Cauchy surface influences the definition of the subalgebra, leading to a reconsideration of traditional methods. We explore alternative approaches to rectify this issue and ensure the reliability of the perturbative framework.

To accurately detect smoke in surgical settings, we propose an advanced deep learning approach that outperforms a recent study within the same field. Although effective, the current best method relies on cumbersome 3D convolutional networks, necessitating a significant amount of computational power and memory. Our research aims to overcome this limitation by introducing a ground-up approach, starting from extracting low-level features from images through a simplified, fully convolutional network, and then forwarding these features to a simplified sequential classification module. The initial part of the network is trained to extract the desired characteristics from surgical images, and the classification module is efficiently trained on smoke and non-smoke dataset. Our method successfully replicates the accuracy of state-of-the-art 3D convolutional networks on two public datasets, achieving notable improvements in classification precision and processing speed. Notably, our two-stream network features comprise only 12,000 parameters, a fraction of the 7.5 million parameters in the comparable 3D convolutional network.

This research investigates the creation of robust molecular entanglement via the Molmer-Sorensen gate, specifically designed to withstand frequency variations common in complex ion chains. Our study provides a unified approach for creating a robust gate structure, and explores the trade-offs between robustness, efficiency, and the capacity to generate multi-qubit entanglement. To compare with traditional linear arrays, we develop a novel concept of 'bottleneck bandwidth', and demonstrate that arranged triangle and tree structures can substantially reduce the required gate bandwidth, while simultaneously enhancing entanglement capabilities. Our findings are equally applicable to other gates utilizing collective oscillations, and could hold significant value for future quantum computing and multi-qubit simulation systems.

Our study employs the reverse Monte Carlo simulation method in conjunction with first-principles calculations to analyze the structures of some ABO3 perovskite systems. The findings reveal that the equilibrium state of these materials is characterized by an off-center position of B-cations, which is influenced by the presence of other ions. The tolerance radius is utilized to quantify the degree of disorder in each system and the role of volume and dopant cation size on B-cation off-centering is examined. The findings also highlight the significance of utilizing three-dimensional frameworks instead of single crystals to study the properties of perovskite materials.

We introduce a novel multivariate Gaussian process that maintains conditional independence between individual processes within a graphical model. Each process is then linked using conditional determinacy, resulting in which the intrinsic stochastic process remains multivariate Gaussian. This framework expands existing methods, specifically extending previously established techniques to higher-dimensional settings. We demonstrate the utility of this framework through a realistic simulation.

Our proposal for using periodic and anti-periodic recurrent neural networks, called Poly-PNN and Alt-PNN, respectively, yields exceptional results in calculating the ground state properties of molecular systems. In a recent empirical study, we found that incorporating recurrent neural networks in a quantum circuit deep learning approach greatly improved accuracy when ground state estimates were based on a small number of quantum samples. To further enhance performance, we implemented Poly-PNN and Alt-PNN, which demonstrated superior results on the Fermi-Hubbard model's ground state and excited energy levels. Notably, our models exhibited a significant 10x reduction in parameters compared to equivalent CNN designs.

A novel, computationally efficient method for convex optimization has been developed through the Generalized Chebyshev method. This approach yields stronger average-case performance than existing techniques like gradient descent, especially for smooth, L-smooth objectives. The average-case complexity of the Generalized Chebyshev method is characterized by a linear dependency on the optimal value and logarithmic complexity in the optimal solution relative to the L-smooth value. Furthermore, a polynomial-time worst-case complexity bound has been obtained for this optimization algorithm.

Moiré heterostructures combining twisted layers of semiconductors create a unique 
environment that modifies the interlayer potential and gives rise to interlayer 
excitons with distinct properties. In this study, we utilize a theoretical model to 
investigate the optical characteristics associated with interlayer excitons and 
gauge the impact of interlayer interactions. Our analysis indicates that these 
interlayer excitons can produce distinctive optical phenomena that vary based 
on stack orientation and intensity of interlayer attraction. Furthermore, this 
study proposes that these materials have the potential to generate robust 
interlayer excitonic states protected by symmetry.

This research focuses on developing advanced algorithms to accurately determine the position and orientation of a mobile agent equipped with adaptive filtering technology, operating in a two-dimensional or three-dimensional environment where adaptability is essential. We introduce a probabilistic data association algorithm that dynamically changes its parameters in real-time to improve positioning accuracy, particularly in the presence of multiple targets. The proposed approach utilizes a Bayesian estimation method to adaptively select measurement associations and calibrate them according to changing conditions, to which a modified Kalman filter is applied to provide real-time position and orientation updates. Our simulation-based evaluation, involving a state-of-the-art true multi-modal target tracking scenario, demonstrates the exceptional performance of our novel algorithm in comparison to existing alternatives.

We've performed an exhaustive analysis of $W$ boson decays into jets, considering multiple interpretations of the "bump" hypothesis within the $pp \to W^{\pm} Z$ triangle. Our research also addresses potential new physics contributing to $W$ boson helicity transitions. We found that the observed joint helicity fractions for polarization states of $W^{\pm}$ and $Z$ bosons aligns with Standard Model predictions, although specific models introducing effective operators yield detectable signatures in certain helicity asymmetries and decay angular distributions. We established the significance of observing the "bump" hypothesis in $pp \to W^+ Z$ at 13 TeV, where the desired event count is too low for a confident detection. Our study stresses the necessity of thoroughly understanding $W$ boson helicity transitions in order to confidently identify novel physics interpretations of the "bump" hypothesis.

A review of the current knowledge on gravity's higher-spin extensions is provided. The focus lies within the class of theories dubbed "Cotton gravity," which are distinguished by the absence of a zero-rest-mass, five-index Cotton tensor field. This field arises naturally as a conformal equivalent of the Weyl field and is indicative of a theory's pure vacuum state. The review begins with an examination of the universal properties of these extensions, particularly their universal symmetries and the constraints imposed by linear fluctuations around the vacuum state. Subsequent sections delve into the conformal equivalent forms of gravity's higher-spin extensions, with a focus on the unique properties of "Rarita-Schwinger" fields and their applications. The final section explores the connection between Cotton gravity and the newly-discovered "new massive gravity" theories, which share striking similarities with the former.

We establish the equivalence of orthomodular lattices and orthomodular spaces by proving that any orthomodular space can be represented by an orthomodular lattice, and conversely, any orthomodular lattice corresponds to an orthomodular space.

Our goal is to obtain proof representations that can be utilized to enhance review processes and make human-provided feedback more efficient. To accomplish this, we develop ProveR, a reasoning machine, to verify the accuracy of mathematical steps in scientific publications. By transforming prodedural elements into graph representations, we create a learning framework to identify errors within these representations. Our approach translates the graph representation into a problem-solving space, where a value network is used to anticipate rewards when certain actions are taken. Through 20,000 test problems, we found that ProveR validated 99.7% of correct steps in Taylor & Francis publications but only 81.8% of steps in unpublished work (noemical). When comparing our results to Automated Reasoning, we found that ProveR solved a variety of verification tasks but struggled with more complex tasks, where Automated Reasoning outperformed us. Following human feedback, we made several adjustments, 'Human in the Loop', which marked a significant improvement in our accuracy, reaching 99.9% and 98.9% in validation and false positives, respectively. Our research identified several areas for further improvement, alongside an updated public code, at https://github.com/gabrath/ProveR.

We analyze the eighth moment of the L-function's power saddle distribution, a complex phenomenon where its density function is expressed as an integral of Lagrange polynomials. Our investigation, however, is aligned with Watson's seminal approach, as well as recent contributions from Soundararajan and Harper. We treat the L-function as a random variable, averaging its values over a specific subset of integers. This subset is defined by a positive integer parameter, n, which we assume is greater than 3. For each n, the subset consists of all positive integers less than or equal to n, multiplied by the square root of their product. This range is closed by the eighth root of its largest element. By employing the Fourier series and an integral representation, we derive several key results. These findings include an analytic expression, verified with computational data, along with an estimate of its rate of convergence. This allows us to reserve the outcomes for even and odd values of the parameter, n. Additionally, we leverage our findings to provide the moments of the L-function's power saddle distribution at arbitrary degrees. Furthermore, our analysis yields the expression in the form of a sum of squares, which may hold utility in broader mathematical contexts.

Preconditioning interior point methods for optimization problem resolution involves incorporating an early inner iteration termination strategy. This technique involves stopping the inner process before convergence to a precise solution, allowing for a more efficient exit from the interior point's iterative cycle. A byproduct of this termination approach is a potentially useful (though less frequently utilized) lower-bound solution, which can be utilized to develop an inequality-constrained model cuttings plane method. A key aspect is a model-centric variance metric that determines and adapts the depth of each iteration's preconditioning: when the variance within the inequality constraints is high, deeper preconditioning is employed to optimize the solution, whereas lower variance is met with more minimal preconditioning as the optimal solution is refined. This cutting plane method was tested on an energy-based model of thermodynamic system equilibrium, with results demonstrating significant speedups – up to 7.5 times faster execution time – when compared to a conventional model not utilizing preconditioning or early termination.

An analytical formula for the transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ is derived at the NLO level in QCD, with the goal of incorporating it into the variable flavor number scheme. This involves introducing a transition region to smoothly switch between $N$-quark and $(N-1)$-quark schemes within QCD. The derived formula is in agreement with the standard NLO transition function and meets all necessary criteria. It is expressed in a way that facilitates the implementation of additional flavor number schemes, and we detail how to incorporate it into the $\overline{\rm MS}$ and Frixione-Lari-Signorini-Mansi schemes.

We present the AI Incident Database, a comprehensive resource that gathers
information about AI systems' malfunctioning episodes, referred to as incidents.
Our goal is to advocate for incident reporting and make available a framework
for recording and analyzing these occurrences, which can lead to enhanced AI
technology. Currently, there is no established system for logging incidents,
and as a result, the broader AI research community has limited understanding of
these events. We believe that collecting and studying incidents could provide
valuable insights and contribute to the advancement of intelligent systems.

A revised version of Ernst's original differential equation for general relativity in conjunction with Yang-Mills theory has been reestablished. The equation's derivation, which disregards the zero-Einstein vector equation, utilizes a novel approach to maintain Yang-Mills invariance. This approach draws analogue methods from the work of North for the general relativity context and relies on a similar strategy to achieve Yang-Mills invariance. The current formulation may be extended to include modifications of Einstein's original theory.

This paper builds upon existing notions of conflict and its resolution in
networked systems, where a monitoring system compares actual behavior to multiple
specifications. We introduce a novel aspect: a conflict resolution mechanism
operating within a monitoring system to resolve conflicts that arise between
specifications as well as within a single specification, all taking into account
the temporal dimensions of the systems in question. A new type of formula is
introduced to express the idea that a run of a system should be consistent with
multiple specifications by potentially selecting one specification as
"canonical" to resolve ambiguities. This new class of formulae is then utilized
to formulate the problem of conflict and resolution in a formal manner and
solutions to these problems are provided, along with an illustration using a
network of traffic lights. The concepts introduced in this work are related to
existing notions in the following areas: (i) comparing runs of a system to
constraints (ii) ensuring a system follows a protocol with multiple processes and
(iii) monitoring a system to ensure it meets a particular specification. The
key distinction lies in these studies' focus on a single run of a system, as
opposed to our consideration of how a monitoring system addresses the various
specifications being compared.

Prototyping quantum circuit design with existing programming languages can be challenging due to differences in the structure of these languages and quantum circuits. To overcome this, the Proto-Quipper-M has been developed, incorporating a quantum circuit-simulating module into the Proto-Quipper family of relational programming languages. Through a series of abstractions, Proto-Quipper-M embeds quantum states and operations within the framework while ensuring the preservation of the non-cloning property for quantum states. Additionally, it provides a compilation framework that allows for the prototype's evaluation on quantum hardware. The current implementation serves as a proof-of-concept and can compile a limited subset of Proto-Quipper-M into OpenQASM. Future developments aim to incorporate error-prone quantum hardware and high-level circuit designs.

We analyze the largest eigenvalues near the spectral edges of three ensembles from the complex symplectic random-matrix class. Utilizing finite-size scaling, we factor the spectral correlations based on mid-spectral behavior. Subsequently, three distinct factors are derived for the truncated Poisson, Laguerre, and Jacobi models. Furthermore, we confer with the Stokes phenomenon to derive the large-size limit of these factors, thereby validating our approach.

Our study introduces a groundbreaking technique for precisely measuring optical phase shifts by leveraging the capabilities of Sagnac interferometry combined with two-mode squeezing devices. The integration of this setup with cutting-edge detection tools enables quantum-enhanced optical phase sensing with remarkable sensitivity, outperforming traditional classical methods. We carefully evaluate the final level of detectability achieved using our proposed setup and demonstrate that the inherent two-mode squeezing in the setup surpasses classical limits, resulting in a substantial advancement in optical phase shift measurement precision.

One of the most efficient algorithms for near-linear time genomic sequence assembly, proposed by Myra Kim and colleagues, relies on multiway number partitioning. Although the underlying partitioning scheme appears intricate, it can be simplified by examining its connection to standard number partitioning methods. Based on this insight, two new algorithms are developed for generating the required partitions, one of which utilizes binary search to achieve the goal in $O(\log n)$ iterations. These results serve as a foundation for the original algorithm's time complexity analysis, ultimately demonstrating its complexity to be no worse than $O(n\log n)$.

We suggest a revised logistic equation that takes into account the temporal advancement of cell populations, and it is based on recent research into nonlinear delay differential equations. This modified equation has certain practical advantages - it is certain to converge to a positive steady state and can be regarded as an advanced version of the Richardson equation. We have established numerical solutions for this new equation, and our results have been supported by practical examples.

Spatio-temporal point processes capture the underlying patterns of event occurrences in various applications. One popular approach to modeling these processes combines Gaussian processes with point process observations, often utilizing the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation to analyze event times on a convex cone space. By doing so, this method offers flexible and interpretable modeling outcomes. Nonetheless, conventional Gaussian process-based models are confined to a limited number of data points due to their practical limitations. This research introduces a new model, called the ILR-GPWP, which combines the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation with a wide-spread Gaussian process wizard patch approach to efficiently model event times only. The ILR-GPWP method demonstrates superior performance compared to the conventional Gaussian Oxford Gaussian process model, the GPWP for real-life and simulated data sets, and also provides a wide-range of practical applications in various domains.

Researchers believe that nanoscale quantum devices, specifically those based on hybrid materials, could be crucial in developing robust quantum computers. A key property of these devices is the ability to pair subelectronic charges into entangled cooperatives, which can induce a ballroom-like current flow. Our research focuses on discovering phenomena related to this induced current flow, particularly as it occurs within nanoscale quantum wells when subjected to external gates. Our study shows that this current flow can be split into two distinct parts, one of which is influenced by the phase of the superconducting partner. This distinction reveals that the phase of the superconducting partner has a greater impact on the entangled cooperatives than previously considered. Our research also reveals that while these entangled cooperatives can resist decoherence, they are not completely immune to it. As such, their realization in nanoscale quantum wells under external gate influence offers an innovative approach for enhancing the entangled cooperatives' resistance to decoherence while also allowing for their programmable and precise manipulation.

The production of the 78Ge isotope was achieved using the RIKEN Radioisotope Beam Factory's combined accelerator and superconducting solenoid Indo system. As part of this study, the nuclear properties of 78Ge were investigated and compared with those of 59Co. The results showed that 78Ge exhibits a more closed nuclear shell structure than 59Co. Additionally, the study found 78Ge to have a nuclear structure similar to that of the proton-rich nucleus 56Ni, suggesting that 78Ge and 56Ni have many nuclear characteristics in common. The study also determined the half-life of 78Ge to be around 0.92 seconds. When compared with theoretical predictions, the experimental data showed some discrepancies, which may indicate the need for further refinement in the theoretical models. Based on this production and identification, the possibility of measuring the half-life of the nearby 78Ge isotope is now considered.

The study focused on measuring extremely short-lived, lightweight isotope
levels near the line of stability. The development of a fast and quick separation
technique using the $B\\ho$-IMS method enabled the detection and study of these
isotopes. The technique utilizes an electric and magnetic field setup to guide and
separate the ions based on different mass-to-charge ratio in a specific area. The
study involved identifying and measuring the levels of 42, 44, 46, 48Al, 46, 48, 50Si, 46, 48Ti, and 44, 46, 48, 50K isotopes
using the RITR optical detector and transport system. The results showed good
agreement with theoretical predictions and other research outcomes.

We propose an innovative approach to capturing U(1) gauge symmetries within the realm of normalizing flows. Through the utilization of a wavefunction that transforms under the action of U(1), we demonstrate the development of a Lagrangian-based on a wavefunction's contrast score. This contrast score defines a potentially minimal energy functional, the optimization of which results in the normalizing flow's parameters optimizing gauge-invariant objectives. We apply this framework to a simple linear chain, where the wavefunction's gauge transformation can be computed exactly, and we demonstrate the method's effectiveness by approximating the Helmholtz-Hamiltonon model.

This research investigates the effectiveness of contextual pre-training, 
decontextualized representation, and matching algorithms in identifying 
text within specific patterns. We find that introducing a contextual component 
enhances the accuracy of pattern recognition beyond solely decontextualized 
approaches. Building on this discovery, we introduce BiasDrone, a technique 
that adjusts the training of visual transformer architectures to better fit 
decontextualized representations. With BiasDrone, these models can be used 
as a flying NLP expert to recognize text in images, yielding the most 
accurate results to date on APTCHA, SEBAPTCHA, and ICDAR 2015-17 challenge 
datasets. Notably, our technique surpasses previous work, including Fine-Tuning 
from Any Angle (FTAA), by achieving a notable 6% improvement on APTCHA.

The top quark production cross-section has been measured in proton-lead and proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV energy, using data collected at the LHC by the ATLAS detector. The measurement involved recording 25.2 fb^-1 of proton-lead and 32.2 fb^-1 of proton-proton data. The results show that the proton-lead cross-section is consistent with expectations from perturbative quantum chromodynamics and is similar to the proton-proton cross-section within statistical uncertainty.

Developing application migration policies for edge servers in thin client scenarios can be challenging due to varying user activities and the absence of real-time database information. In this research, a context-aware framework is proposed to streamline application migration and improve execution efficiency. The proposed framework utilizes a context-aware migration policy that considers user interaction, system resources, and the duration of inactivity. Additionally, a context-aware migration strategy is developed to handle unforeseen circumstances, such as system failures or changes in user behavior. The research presents two context-aware migration approaches, including a static approach based on predefined rules and a dynamic approach in real-time via an Orchestration Database. The performance of the proposed framework and comparison of its performance with existing solutions, specifically the NICE migration policy, demonstrate significantly improved execution accuracy and agility. The evaluation revealed that the successful execution rate of the proposed framework was 94.62% and could be scaled to handle 317.62 migrations per second.

We've conducted an in-depth examination of angular cluster statistics for galaxies at 179 MHz from the LoTSS survey. The observed galaxies align with the predictions of the ΛCDM cosmology up to a certain threshold of signal-to-noise ratio. However, our measurements show slightly higher angular power spectrum levels compared to previous findings. Upon accounting for blinding effects, the remaining discrepancies still persist. To understand these discrepancies better, a simplified model incorporating blinding artifacts was proposed and demonstrated to work reasonably well for S/N > 3. The remaining difficulties might be resolved once blinding assumptions are thoroughly validated.

We introduce an efficient, adaptable algorithm to tackle the rank-lasso problem effectively in high-dimensional settings. It mitigates the drawbacks of existing methods by reducing computational cost, cutting down dependence on unlabeled data, and eliminating the need for parameter tuning. Our adaptive-sieving-based approach offers model-specific and data-driven estimation of support size without requiring initial estimates, thus overcoming critical challenges in solving the rank-lasso problem. Empirical evaluations on various datasets demonstrate our method's superior performance compared to established benchmarks.

Although the average rate of entropy production in optimal protocols approaches a unique asymptotic value for large time intervals, the sequence of optimal protocols does not converge uniformly, which indicates a lack of uniqueness. This discrepancy is resolved by examining the sequence of the natural parameter in the Lagrangian function used in the optimization process and demonstrating that the optimal protocol achieves the global minimum when the natural parameter equals the average entropy production rate. This result not only confirms the existence of a unique global optimal protocol but also serves as the foundation for proving the convergence of the sequence of optimal protocols in the stronger sense of almost everywhere convergence.

The growing influence of AI services necessitates a more comprehensive understanding of their environmental impact, extending beyond the technical considerations of computer hardware and software. This study develops an innovative approach to assess the environmental consequences of AI services across their entire lifespan, focusing on the interconnectedness of AI components and data. This research presents: 1) a novel framework for AI service life cycle analysis, 2) an operational method for calculating environmental impacts, and 3) practical assessment tools. This framework is then utilized to evaluate the environmental effects of four real-world AI services. This assessment sheds light on the individual and combined environmental impacts of model deployment, data preprocessing, training, and data acquisition. The results of this study can inform developers and users about potential environmental consequences, fostering the creation of more sustainable AI services. This research may serve as a foundation for future investigations into the environmental implications of AI services.

Up to now, most process monitoring methods have been concerned with descriptive analysis, providing an understanding of the current process state, but little has been done in a prescriptive manner, offering recommendations for improvement. While some prescriptive methods have been developed, they often rely on simulated data, lacking real-world practicality. This work aims to close the gap by introducing a rigorous evaluation framework for prescriptive process monitoring, leveraging real-world industrial data. We also report on several limitations of current monitoring methods, including the potential for suboptimal recommendations due to the challenge of identifying an activity's actual goal, the absence of activity goal detection, and the limitations of certain optimization techniques, all of which we believe to be inherent characteristics of current techniques.

A novel approach to error assessment is developed for coupled solutions to fluid dynamics equations using the dual-weighted residual method. Initially, weak forms of residual estimates are derived from weak couplings in coupled problems. Furthermore, a dual-weighted residual method is formulated within a mixed finite element framework, enabling estimation of coupled problem residuals without requiring exact solutions to sub-problems. Numerical demonstrations involve solving coupled Navier-Stokes and Darcy equations in various domains to evaluate the accuracy of estimated errors.

Graph packing is an important area of study, but certain graph packing problems have proven elusive to bound tightly. Due to their relationship with vertex-disjoint paths, circuits and cycles in graph packing have seen significant attention. Past work yielded a lower bound of O(r(n)) for vertex-disjoint circuits, where n is the number of vertices and r(v) is the packing number of a given graph v. Utilizing a novel approach, a lower bound of o(r(n)) is achieved for vertex-disjoint circuits in graphs without long cycles. Additionally, a linear upper bound is established for packing independent streams of vertex-disjoint circuits in graphs without long cycles, along with a linear upper bound for independent sets of vertex-disjoint paths. This work also explores linear bounds for independent streams of vertex-disjoint paths in d-regular graphs.

We examine the formation of opinions among a large group of people whose individual perspectives exist within a one-dimensional space. Each person initially holds his own unique opinion, which is either fixed or can change over time, akin to a magnetic spin. Our system draws inspiration from those used in statistical physics to study ferromagnetism, but with a focus on the dynamics of opinion formation. As time progresses and interactions are established between individuals, the initial random organization of the group gives rise to distinct social cliques characterized by uniformly held opinions within each clique. The collective movement of these opinion groups is governed by a single parameter that seeks to minimize the average distance between individuals within each clique. Despite being unable to represent all aspects of real-life opinion interactions, our system successfully replicates the widespread separation of social groups seen in everyday life.

We've investigated black holes characterized by a scalar field with multiple symmetries, both in their overall properties and when a specific field equation holds in a specific limit. This research was inspired by similarities between these properties and those observed in holographic superconductors. We've derived an approximate equation for a specific type of black hole by incorporating elements of the nonlinear, power-law corrected holographic superconductors, which matches a previously derived equation for another type of black hole. Additionally, we've analyzed thermodynamic properties of these black holes.

The process of producing mature mRNA from DNA involves a significant time lag.
This research quantifies the transcription delay by analyzing the distribution of
mRNA completion times in two models: one for a single gene with varying transcription
rates, and another for a population of genes with a distribution of transcription rates.
In the first model, the distribution of mRNA completion times is solved analytically,
and the result matches the average delay to within 10% even for short transcripts.
However, this approximation breaks down for very short transcripts in the second model. 
To resolve this discrepancy, the transcription delay is approximated as a sum of chasms
duration in a third model, which involves a population of genes with a distribution of
transcription rates. This approach provides a precise and general measure of the delay
but requires knowledge of the transcription rate distribution.

The excitation energies of even-parity 0+ and 2+ states in 64Ni nucleus have been studied using the 58Fe (+$d$) reaction at 52 MeV. Despite having no low-lying state in the final, cross-section patterns revealed that 64Ni possesses a distinct energy range for 0+ and 2+ excitations. By applying the Monte Carlo shell model, it was discovered that the distribution of excitation energies is influenced by the N = 40 subshell gap and the monopole interaction, leading to 64Ni's excitation energies being lower than those of 62Ni and 66Ni. The breakdown of the 40 $ igoplus$ 20 core structure also emerged as a significant factor.

We're investigating anomaly patterns in SU(N) gauge theories that incorporate extra Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation. These additional fermions are given the labels vij in a general case, with specific scenarios involving 2Nf, 16, 32f, 32ad, and 32b types. Our study builds on previous research of similar types and includes a broader range of fermion content. We've established various combination rules for the anomalies, expressed in various forms, and also found relationships among various 'index' theorems as well as connections to earlier works by Andree, Plefka, Schenkel, and their counterparts.

We establish that for any group code C, its dual code D per C is equivalent to a group code $\widetilde{D}^{\perp}$ produced by extending the group $G/N$ of quotients of the group N, which is the kernel of the group homomorphism having domain G and ranging over a cyclic group Z/nZ for some integer n. Additionally, we determine the equivalence transformations that convert D to $\widetilde{D}^{\perp}$, and we show that the codes C and D are equivalent to each other if and only if their dual codes D and D per C are equivalent.

Bucket Elimination is a general framework for inferences and optimizations in graphical models, and its core idea involves eliminating variables one by one using propagation to reduce a given problem to a more manageable size. When applied to Bayesian Networks, Bucket Elimination often enters an infinite loop due to its inability to make progressive reductions, which is caused by the absence of a child-sibling parent variable configuration for each variable being eliminated. We address this limitation by introducing a novel variant of Bucket Elimination, called Elimination with Efficient Time Complexity, or ETX Bucket Elimination, which is inspired by the efficient time-critical search algorithm. We then apply this new etx-BE technique to Bayesian Networks and prove that it has a guaranteed finite termination, in addition to deriving key properties and providing a step-by-step description of the etx-BE algorithm through a detailed example.

To navigate complex environments such as indoor and outdoor spaces, it is essential to respond to changes in one's surroundings by recognizing and dropping or picking up objects. Picking up an object involves integrating visual, kinematic, and gravitational information to identify a dropped object, incorporating sensory data to refine this assessment. We draw on physical principles, specifically gravity-driven dynamics, to develop a simple model that "feels" for dropped objects through the behavior of a virtual agent. The virtual agent is capable of adjusting its sensitivity to gravity to detect any discrepancies in its drop trajectory, pinpointing the source of the discrepancy to determine the location of the dropped object. We present a public dataset called the Drop-Picking Dataset, consisting of a batch of simulations in 2D environments, designed to test the model's performance and identify areas for improvement. Through drop-picking simulations, our approach successfully demonstrates the ability to accurately locate objects in a variety of scenarios.

This study provides the first comprehensive theoretical and numerical analysis of frictional jamming in two-dimensional arrays of disks under stress confined to one phase. Our research reveals that the point of frictional jamming occurs at a stress-independent threshold modulus, but differs substantially from the frictionless jamming scenario. In particular, our results indicate that the exponents governing the flow properties in frictionally jammed packs are distinct from those observed in frictionless conditions. Notably, our theoretical model accurately predicts an exponential decline in modulus with inverse pressure, in accordance with previous experimental findings. Additionally, our research offers a novel, simplified approach to estimating jamming points in systems where stress and pressure are not in equilibrium.

A novel AR model is proposed, where the AR coefficients and order are determined by minimizing the Akaike information criterion with a smoothness penalty. The model's performance exceeds that of a standard AR model on historical US electricity demand data, as quantified by several key metrics. A concise review of time series forecasting and the underlying machine learning concepts is provided to facilitate understanding of the proposed method.

As critical stakeholders, public sector professionals need to be informed about the potential
algorithmic biases in Web search results, which could compromise their professional decisions.
This research provides an overview of the existing discussions surrounding online search
bias, highlighting the diverse perspectives and approaches to identifying and addressing this
issue. By discussing the fundamental challenges posed by the complex and interdisciplinary
nature of the problem, this paper aims to provide a systematic framework for understanding
the various methods and tools available to detect search bias and promote awareness of their
implementation and utility.

Our study focuses on evaluating the program synthesis framework from the perspective of a hypothetical user who seeks to solve a specific functional problem. We utilize the concept of inverse semigroups to represent possible programs and their relationships, and then establish a user-centric perspective to assess the synthesis efficiency and feasibility. Average-case performance under this perspective is analyzed by employing two widely used probability distributions on the set of inverse semigroups. Notably, under the uniform distribution, our results demonstrate that the synthesis framework can generate a program within a reasonably small time frame, specifically no more than 10^8 steps on average. In contrast, under the counting measure distribution, the synthesis time is significantly higher at around 10^370 steps on average. These findings offer a more nuanced understanding of the program synthesis capability, suggesting that the average synthesis time is still manageable but may be excessively high for some practical scenarios.

To tackle environmental issues like global warming, it's crucial to gain deeper insights into the complex Earth system to inform precise projections about its future behavior. Researchers have been using model reductions to analyze and understand certain aspects of the Earth's climate dynamics, which involve intricate interactions between atmospheric, oceanic, and land processes. These reductions rely on specific parametrization schemes that represent how different components of the Earth system affect each other. By applying an advanced mathematical technique called Tikhonov regularization to these models, researchers have been able to simplify them while maintaining their qualitative behavior. This breakthrough enables the development of new, more effective reduction methods that can reveal the Earth's climate state and ultimately lead to more accurate predictions and projections.

JCMT/ALMA Sure Successor, a next-generation submillimeter telescope, is being developed at a junction of technological advancements. Featuring a 3-meter diameter telescope, it will utilize an advanced, lightweight design using materials like carbon fiber and incorporate an optomechanical system with a moving secondary mirror and wavemaker. This design is optimized for versatility in chemical composition observations, especially in the far-infrared range with high spatial resolution using a device called Frequency Agile Receiver for Gravitational wave Observations (FARGO). The FARGO instrument will facilitate the observation of fine structure lines in the infrared spectrum, giving scientists access to key signals including oxygen and hydrogen from kilonovae. By pairing with a ground-pumping system, the telescope will be capable of observing frequencies between 30 and 110 GHz. Development of the FARGO instrument will prioritize low-noise performance, with aim of attaining 70-100 GHz system noise levels below 10 millikelvin. Throughout its development, the FARGO team will maintain compatibility with existing ALMA and JCMT Receiver System Utilization Agreements. Upon completion in 2023, the FARGO team will conduct initial testing in 2023 and 2024 at the JCMT, followed by on-altaz at the ALMA by 2025. Following this, the FARGO team will conduct the Final Test at the ALMA by 2026. Following this, the FARGO team will conduct the science verification at the AL

We aim to develop a data-driven approach for real-time X-ray beam adjustment in the treatment of cancer. The current method involves delivering X-ray beams in predetermined patterns without accomodating daily changes in patient position. To address this limitation, our model uses data from fluoroscopy images to adjust the treatment beams in real-time. The key challenge is creating our model using simulated data from synthetic treatment plans. To test its effectiveness, we applied the model in a simulated scenario of treating a phantom, with the goal of accurately localizing the phantom's position using only data from the adjusted X-ray beams. The results demonstrated the model's ability to efficiently estimate the phantom's position in real-time, without requiring significant computational resources. To evaluate the model's performance, we used both synthetic and actual data from an in-vivo treatment protocol, with the outcome showing close agreement with the reference values. Specifically, the mean absolute error in estimating the phantom's position using the model was around 0.7 mm.

Compositional, high-dimensional data can be characterized by several features: parts that span the entire range from 0 to 1, coherent parts within the 'whole', and only a few significant interactions. This type of data is frequently encountered in fields like environmental, biological, social, and material science studies. Due to the total mass constraint in these datasets, the standard analytical methods face challenges. This chapter focuses on the application of compositional data analysis and embedding techniques to uncover hidden patterns within these datasets. We have chosen two practical case studies to illustrate this: the analysis of air pollution in Valencia, Spain, and the investigation of COVID-19 deaths in European countries. These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of using real-valued vector representations for predictive tasks and facilitating task execution, such as clustering, classification, and regression, on these dataset vectors.

Recent studies using stellar radiation-hydrodynamic simulations and detailed
atmospheric models have made predictions about the properties of giant planets
under various stellar environments. These results highlight the significance of
combining observational data with theoretical models to gain insight into the
formation and evolution of exoplanets. A pivotal aspect of understanding
planetary formation is explaining why most planets are small and others are
massive. Runaway gas accretion, a key process in planetary formation, can be
informed by observing planetary masses and separations. To assess its
validity, we used Occam's principle to compare observed distributions of
exoplanets with the predictions of theoretical models. These predictions were
based on simulations of core accretion and gas accretion, also taking into
account the effects of gravitational fragmentation and pebble accretion. Compared
to core accretion, models that allow for runaway gas accretion and final mass
determinations by tidal interactions with the parent star, overpredicted mass
ratios and underpredicted separations relative to observations. When high-cadence
spatial distributions were considered, none of the theoretical distributions
matched the observations, and a curve featuring smaller planets and fewer hot
Jupiters aligned less well with the data than a comparable distribution featuring
smaller planet masses and more distant giant planets. Combining these results with
the predictions of pebble accretation models, which also allow for runaway gas

In episodic memory tasks, agents navigate multiple environments to find a specific piece of information, and their performance relies on keeping track of unobserved states and past experiences to make accurate predictions from limited data. Our research focuses on EPOM-MDPs, a model for handling partial reinforcement learning with an agent having access to limited observation windows of its state. We propose a new algorithm, E-Memory Power, to enhance an agent's prediction accuracy and reveal its significance in unknown state tracking. Our findings show that our method has the capacity to learn an optimal solution on specific task types, and we provide further evidence through theoretical analysis and experimental results that enhances our understanding of dynamic memory in partial observation settings.

A feeble interaction between the hidden sector and the Standard Model can be characterized by a dark matter candidate and several mediator particles, which may primarily interact with each other. To investigate the properties of this dark matter candidate, we consider two scenarios: (a) the mass of the mediator particles is significantly smaller than the dark matter mass, and (b) the mass of the mediator particles is only slightly greater than the dark matter mass. In the first case, the interaction between the dark matter and the mediator particles forms a complex resonant structure, which can lead to substantial enhancement of the elastic scattering cross section and correct interpretation of recent astrophysical data. In the second case, the role of the mediator particles is analogous to that of the gauge bosons in the visible sector, and the distribution of the resonance, characterized by the transition to a dark matter pair, plays a crucial part in determining the kinematical parameter space.

We introduce Mod-Cog, an online cognitive battery that offers a diverse range of
cognitive tasks beyond what's currently available. Building on existing research,
Mod-Cog combines three classes of tasks - perceptual, reasoning, and language -
with a wide variety of question types and moderate difficulty levels. In contrast
to other more complex batteries, Mod-Cog is designed for use on common household
devices and can be completed in under two hours with a reward incentive. To
establish its reliability and validity, we conducted a study with one hundred
participants, along with a code development and pre registration, available at
osf.io/zjhgc. Mod-Cog is now freely accessible (osf.io/yd94f) and we encourage
researchers to utilize it in their studies to develop artificial intelligence
capable of addressing real-world cognitive challenges.

We analyze the geometric representations of nilpotent algebras, focusing on their exponential types. Specifically, we investigate the properties of the varieties corresponding to such algebras: their dimensionality, uniqueness, and relationship to the stabilizer subalgebras. We demonstrate that for most exponential types, the varieties associated with nilpotent algebras are distinct and have lower dimensions compared to their non-nilpotent counterparts. However, for a specific type, T, where the stabilizer subalgebra exhibits a particular structure, the variety corresponding to the corresponding stabilizer subalgebra is shown to be a subset of the variety corresponding to the full algebra. Moreover, in this case, the dimensionality difference between the two is found to be one, and various concrete examples are provided to illustrate these findings.

Large-scale, kiloparsec-jet structures are observed throughout the universe, typically powered by inverse Compton interaction between relativistic electrons and cosmic microwave background photons. The inverse Compton interaction gives rise to hard X-ray radiation, which has been identified as a prominent feature of these jets. The electromagnetic jet model proposes that the electrons in these jets become even more relativistic by absorbing energy from magnetic fluctuations, leading to increased inverse Compton emission. The increased efficiency of inverse Compton emission results in X-ray radiation being emitted in the jet, but not in the surrounding intergalactic medium. This, in conjunction with existing observations, provides support for the electromagnetic jet model.

Tadmor's "pre-non-relativistic" parametrization provides an effective way to analytically solve general relativity equations by expanding variables in a specific way. This method was initially outlined in various papers, but a crucial step was only described in a later paper. We follow the standard procedure to use TNR coordinates in the framework of Tadmor's work and then use different methods to achieve accurate numerical solutions with arbitrary precision using mathematical tools. Specifically, we use a formal series to rewrite Einstein's equations in a first-order context and subsequently use a zero-residue condition to derive formal series solutions. Alternatively, we use the LaGrange-Green variational principle to derive formal series solutions in a direct manner. Both methods validate the pre-non-relativistic parametrization as a viable tool for solving Einstein's equations.

A versatile medical image registration technique, SIFT-CPD image registration, is developed to tackle diverse organizational structures across differing modalities and tissues. This approach utilizes scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) descriptors, which are then grouped into probability distribution functions and matched to yield optimal image alignment. The technique is robust to variations in image intensity, and its ability to adapt to unique pixel patterns makes it effective even in the presence of irregularities or incomplete data. The SIFT-CPD image registration method is implemented in open-source C++ code and is successfully applied to register ultrasound images with either X-ray or MRI images, utilizing either point set or image-based correspondence to yield optimal results. The associated journal article is supplemented by additional information and source code, available at https://khe2019.si.edu/sift-cpd/.

We identify the first known instance of an eclipsing detached binary system composed of two white dwarfs, specifically SDSS J082239.54+304857.19. The combination of its substantial eclipse depth and relatively accessible orbit makes this system particularly notable. The determined orbital parameters are as follows: period (P) equals 1.037637 days, eccentricity (e) equals 0.103, and periastron (ω) equals 90 degrees. The analyzed light curve reveals two distinct breaks, suggesting that these white dwarfs are of roughly equal size and separated by an average distance of approximately 4.65 R$_{\odot}$. The estimated absolute magnitudes are consistent with both stars being an SDW with a temperature of 10,000 K. The study shows that this eclipsing double white dwarf binary system is one of the hottest known of its kind, and also features one of the smallest known separations between its component stars.

In deep learning, overfitting is a significant challenge that can be tackled in
the early stages of training using various regularization techniques, including
pooling. Prior research on universal pooling layers revealed their effectiveness
in reducing overfitting and improving performance, including when used with
transfer learning. However, the existing universal pooling methods had one or
more of the following limitations: their theoretical underpinnings were not fully
explained in terms of reducing the growth of neural network weights; they were
only tested with pre-trained networks; and they incorporated transfer learning
parameters, which could lead to overfitting. In response to these shortcomings,
we introduce the UOT-Pooling framework, which is grounded in theoretical justifications
for reducing the growth of neural network weights and can be used with or
without transfer learning. The proposed method is a linear combination of
universal pooling and exclusion operators, and its exclusion part can be seen
as a form of soft regularization. The framework was tested on 11 image
classification datasets, and the results show that it outperforms the existing
universal pooling methods, including the state-of-the-art approaches, when
evaluated on a wide range of learning rates and batch sizes. The UOT-Pooling
framework is available at https://github.com/yassineghoul/uot_pooling.

We analyzed the orientation of 47 active galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey that correspond to different stages of black hole growth. These active galaxies were matched with their host spiral or elliptical galaxies based on stellar mass, and further classified into various Hubble types. We found that distinct distributions of black hole activity correspond to different host galaxy types, and are linked to their underlying structural characteristics. Specifically, more massive black holes are found in galaxies with well-defined bars, and those without a prominent bar tend to have less massive black holes. In contrast, those with a bar but a central bulge, as well as those with a central ring, tend to have moderately massive black holes. These findings suggest that bar dynamics play a key role in shaping the structure of these active galaxies and their subsequent black hole growth.

In this work, we establish a connection between the pointwise 1-type Gauss map of a general rotation surface in three-dimensional Euclidean space and its geometric properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that the pointwise 1-type Gauss map of a general rotation surface is constant if and only if the surface is flat. Furthermore, we provide a distinct characterization of spherical surfaces via their pointwise 1-type Gauss map.

Reconstructing 3D scenes from multiple images requires significant computation.
If we assume that learning monocular depth estimation is cheaper than training for object classification, it makes sense to use computer vision data involving complex 3D scenes more efficiently by focusing on reconstruction instead of classification.
Our approach to low-priority tasks involves introducing noise to make solving the task more challenging without affecting the ordering of ground-truth solutions.
We found that deep neural networks can be trained on low-priority tasks in parallel to a high-priority task, and when resources become scarce, allowing the high-priority task to solve the augmented problem yields improved results.
We verified our approach by designating depth estimation as the high-priority task and object classification as a low-priority task, and found that the method enhances performance and conserves resources without necessitating additional training data.

This work introduces TCube, a time-series data generation framework that tackles the challenge of limited annotated data. Unlike other methods, TCube combines automatic data labeling with a cubic structure to efficiently produce labeled pairs for task-specific transfer learning. By employing a multi-task transformer encoder, TCube can adapt to various time-series tasks and provide reliable semi-supervised performance benchmarks. Furthermore, TCube's design enables it to produce out-of-distribution data, preventing overfitting and providing a better understanding of time-series data characteristics. TCube is particularly beneficial when dataset size and annotated samples are limited, and we showcase its effectiveness using Cuvene, a complex real-world video processing task, where we demonstrate state-of-the-art results on two public datasets.

These studies estimate and compare observables related to rare processes in $B_s^0$ and $B^0$ decayed into muon pairs, incorporating the most recent data from ATLAS and CMS. Specifically, muon pair production rates, matrix element variables, and flavor tagging information were analyzed to determine the sign and magnitude of direct $CPT$-violating and lepton-flavor-violating phenomena, as well as other oblique $CPT$-violating effects. Multiple theoretical models were evaluated to predict direct $Cpt$-violating and extra flavour violating couplings given various constraints. Furthermore, a brief overview of recently published results in $B_s^0$ muon pair decays is provided, including results with varying hadronic form factor parameters. Finally, results from exploring the impact of taste violation on muon pair decay processes in lattice QCD are presented.

We investigate the Ising model on a Cayley tree graph within the framework of group representations, where the group in question is either Z2 or Z3. We derive specific representation formulas for this setup and examine various properties of the model.

The study presents an investigation of the metric on a Kähler manifold that arises from the symplectic form and connection on the manifold, focusing specifically on its implications for the hyperbolic equation. It is demonstrated that the metric contributes to the loss of regularity in the solutions. Utilizing an integral formula for the solutions, the study establishes an sharp estimate for the solutions in L^p spaces. As a result, the study derives the existence and uniqueness of the boundary value problem under certain non-integrable initial conditions. Additionally, the study discusses the decay rate of the solutions in the case of integrable initial conditions.

This research focuses on applying an LSTM-like method to achieve Japanese word segmentation using character-based models. Given the complex nature of Japanese words, which can consist of multiple characters, we aimed to improve segmentation accuracy by utilizing an LSTM-based approach, building on the work of Nishiyama et al. from 2014. Our results demonstrate that this method results in significantly higher accuracy rates compared to conventional approaches, with an overall error reduction of approximately 50%. Additionally, we found that combining LSTM with a linear classifier leads to further enhancements, yielding a 56% decrease in error rates. Our findings indicate that LSTM-based models are a valuable tool for Japanese word segmentation and can potentially be extended to other morphologically complex languages.

Our research involves examining the knowledge links within the Stack Overflow dataset. Stack Overflow is the largest platform for programming-related knowledge sharing, where experts collaborate to develop reliable knowledge through community feedback and revision. Previous studies on knowledge graph-based approaches have successfully answered certain queries, but they didn't explore other important queries. Our work sheds light on the most frequently shared resources, most popular knowledge areas, and the structure of knowledge graphs within Stack Overflow. Our experiments also compare the effectiveness of knowledge graph-based and traditional vector-based methods in answering query-related tasks. Our work is particularly relevant as knowledge graph embedding has gained significant attention in the knowledge graph domain. Our research is significant as it is the first to utilize knowledge graph embedding on an software-related knowledge graph. Our work is important as it highlights the need for utilizing knowledge graph embeddings in answering query-related tasks within software-related knowledge graphs. Our work is motivated by the need to improve software-related knowledge graph quality.

We introduce a computational model to simulate the density profiles of dark matter halos
within a galaxy, using data on galaxy rotation curves. This model accounts for the
presence of a warm core at the center of the halo and a smooth, isothermal core.
By doing so, we're able to simulate the density profiles of dark matter halos for any
given galaxy rotation curve, without needing a pre-defined profile. This approach
accommodates rotation curves with or without a core and features characteristic dips.
By utilizing Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, we evaluate our model's performance
in conjunction with randomly generated galaxy rotation curves. Our results indicate
that, in the absence of true signal, our model will yield approximately 50% false
positives when detecting the diversity of galaxy rotation curves, irrespective of the
presence or absence of a core. Furthermore, our model's framework is adaptable to
different applications in astrophysics, including radial velocity profiles and images
derived from lensing data.

Despite numerous scientific studies, climate change remains poorly understood by the general public, including essential concepts like global warming, which leads to reduced personal actions to combat its effects. This research aims to develop an innovative, values-based approach for conveying climate change information, as prior science communication methods have proven insufficient.
