A proposed system will utilize machine learning to connect individuals' core values with relevant climate information, stimulating more effective values-related actions against climate change. A vulnerability framework will enable scientists to pinpoint and address the personal and institutional barriers preventing climate action by highlighting the inherent risks and benefits specific to each value. This research will explore the technical feasibility of this strategy and explore its potential to revolutionize climate communication, as well as serve as a model for applying AI-driven values-based solutions to address complex societal issues.

Significant advancements have been made in using deep learning to extract symptoms from electronic health records (EHRs), which has contributed to improved performance through domain generalization. Despite this, current techniques still struggle with extracting full patient symptoms due to the difficulty of creating a universal generalization target. To address this challenge, a new approach is presented that bypasses the need for a generalization target by using a universal prior learned through adversarial training. By incorporating adversarial EHR embeddings, existing domain-adaptation models can easily be modified to achieve better performance. Our method has achieved remarkable results, surpassing state-of-the-art performance in substantial margin on three publicly available EHR datasets.

Autonomous vehicles operate under conditions of partial observability, where their sensors have limited visibility of the surroundings. This challenges their ability to make accurate predictions and decisions in dynamic environments, especially when faced with unexpected events such as unexpected pedestrian crossings. This research investigates the capacity of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to learn and anticipate the vehicle's partial history, in order to forecast its future behavior and make informed predictions about the effectiveness of basic safety features like forward collision warning. To achieve this, we develop a simplified simulation environment that models the vehicle's partial observability and the dynamics of its movement, as well as the vehicle's action-space and a performance metric that evaluates the accuracy of its predictions. This is further validated by an examination of the impact of various system components on the RNN's performance, resulting in key insights that can guide the design of predictive auto-manipulation systems for the vehicle.

In the realm of artificial neural networks, specifically in classification tasks, our research introduces a novel neural network architecture that can be both densely connected and trainable. It has the capability to match the performance of high accuracy, traditional ANNs while utilizing significantly fewer bytes per weight. This new architecture can achieve a parameter efficiency of 0.067 bytes per weight when achieving 94% accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset, surpassing the previous best efficiency of 0.078 bytes per weight. Additionally, our research focuses on the classification of MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Our proposed architecture is a sparse, compact neural network where 1) individual neurons can have multiple input connections, and 2) multiple neurons can be connected to a single input point, resembling the synaptic pruning phenomenon where removal of irrelevant connections refines the connections over time. This contrasts with the traditional annealing process where connections are incorporated from the beginning. Our model's performance and efficiency are demonstrated through numerical results on the mentioned datasets.

This research investigates the properties of a specific type of quark matter under the influence of a powerful magnetic field. The study utilizes a theoretical framework, known as the color dielectric approach, in order to analyze its properties. The results show that the presence of a strong magnetic field has a significant impact on the matter's state equation, particularly at higher densities. Furthermore, the presence of a strange quark results in the formation of a more stable phase of matter, which could potentially exist in the cores of neutron stars. The study also examines how the matter's state equation is affected by spin polarization and finds that it has a significant impact on its properties. The results of the research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of quark matter under intense magnetic fields.

Research in Computer Science is shifting towards Single Device Experimentation due to rising concerns over privacy. Conducting computational tasks on a single device is the most secure option. Pando is a novel, cloud-free, distributed computing framework that enables doing computations on multiple machines while starting them all from a single, personal device. It uses the distributed memory model, dividing each calculation into numerous small pieces which are then sent to individual machines for processing and storing in their local memory. If one machine malfunctions or becomes inaccessible, Pando automatically redistributes any affected pieces to another available machine. Thanks to its decentralized design and lack of reliance on a central server, Pando provides an innovative solution for doing large-scale, distributed computing over local networks. Comparing it to running computations on a single, powerful device shows that Pando can significantly boost computational performance, with execution times for some tasks being three to six times faster than using a single device. Additionally, Pando demonstrates better fault-tolerance and reliability than existing, cloud-based distributed computing systems, such as Spark, by achieving faster task completion times and running on fewer devices compared to manually replicating and redistributing task data.

A novel adaptive technique is proposed to optimize the computation of eigenvalues using a range of standard numerical methods. By harnessing the adaptive sampling method, the mesh and, consequently, the solution are dynamically adjusted at each iteration based on the maximum error in the previous solution. This novel approach is contrasted with traditional adaptive methods that focus solely on reducing the error. Furthermore, the adaptive technique is utilized to efficiently evaluate eigenpairs and several benchmark problems, yielding superior results in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

We investigate the intermediate beta-transformations $T_b$ with non-integer base values, and we find that the set of numbers with periodic orbits under $T_b$ consists of numbers in the form of $0._{b}d_1d_2\ldots$ where each digit string $d_1d_2\ldots$ has a length of $k$, and the continued fraction coefficients of $b-1$ repeat indefinitely with a similar structure. Additionally, we use the properties of $T_b$ to categorize badly approximable numbers in non-integer bases and show that they conform to a specific pattern of digit sequences in base $b$.

We determine the low-energy dynamics of $SO(N_c)$ gauge theories with fundamental matter by introducing a clear power counting criterion that distinguishes between the intrinsic U(N_F) chiral symmetry and the approximate SU(N_F) symmetry derived from it. By analyzing the underlying physics, we find that certain quark bilinears contribute to the symmetry breaking, whereas others preserve it. Consequently, this analysis leads us to the conclusion that certain theories may not be fully symmetrical, a realization that allows the use of SU(N_F) symmetry as a useful approximate principle in constructing the effective theories of these systems. We also explore the implications of this finding on the constraints of flavor-dependent gauge theta terms and the possible degenerate vacua that may arise when N_c < N_F.

Our research introduces a novel data visualization known as Disentangled Attribution Curves, which reveals insightful connections between multiple predictive models. These curves illustrate how individual data points interact with multiple models and highlight (1) coinciding and non-coinciding patterns, (2) discrepancies among predictive outputs, and (3) uncertain or ambiguous inputs. We apply the Disentangled Attribution Curves to a well-known dataset related to bike-sharing demand, utilizing graphical models to gain deeper insights into the data and enhance the understanding of attribution analysis. The visualizations uncover important patterns, such as the impact of holidays and weather on bike-sharing demand, and highlight differences between competing prediction methods. Our method can be adapted to various attribution techniques and future research may apply it to continuous data attributes.

Federated learning allows a centralized server to coordinate a collaborative global model across multiple clients while maintaining their local data's privacy. Existing research has focused on two key approaches: one, which relies on statistical analysis to protect privacy, yet often results in inconsistent statistical samples when combining models, and two, which utilizes secure multiplication and addition but falls short due to the need for expensive cryptographic operations. In light of these challenges, this study proposes a novel, efficient approach to tackle the centralised federated learning issue. Our approach, called QuantVal, is built on top of the VMM scheme and leverages fixed-bit quantitative arithmetic to address the aforementioned problem. It relies on the evaluation of finite field polynomials, which are then mapped to quantitative values, ultimately facilitating efficient arithmetic operations on unreliable wireless channels and cryptographically-secured data exchanges between clients and the server. Our results demonstrate that QuantVal necessitates a minimal computational investment, with a computational time of merely 2.4% compared to the conventional MM approach, in addition to producing trustworthy results for all common machine learning metrics.

To bring automated driving to microcontrollers, our concept involves
streamlining the testing process. Current approaches test individual software
components in isolation, but we propose an innovative testing method that
combines device driver functionality with independent software components
(ISCs) on a unified testing framework. When a vehicle's device drivers receive
input from ISC simulations, their coordinated output is then evaluated by an
external judge, facilitating efficient testing of complex system interactions.
Our solution was verified using a real-world application on a vehicle microscope
and was found to be compatible with existing automated testing tools without
requiring additional software setup. As a result, our solution has the potential
to significantly reduce the time and resources required for testing vehicle
device drivers.

We present Timeloops, a CLAMP-based kernel filter for system calls that supports modern languages like C++, Java, Python, and PHP. To handle system calls in languages that use interpretation, such as PHP and Python, Timeloops dynamically intercepts and inspects code execution by creating an abstract representation of the code, allowing it to grant or deny system access on a per-process basis. Timeloops offers a policy framework that enables the isolation of specific system calls for selected processes or groups of processes. Additionally, Timeloops provides a user-space component that enables the testing and development of system call policies before they take effect in the kernel. Its user-space component also facilitates the rewriting of system calls, allowing it to be utilized in scenarios beyond traditional system call filtering. We discuss the design and implementation of Timeloops and demonstrate its capabilities through a demonstration that involves the denial of access to the /proc filesystem for specific processes.

Our research delves into utilizing low-dimensional representations of data to enhance classification capabilities, particularly for single-cell RNA-seq data. We examined various techniques for creating these representations, including traditional Euclidean space methods and more advanced techniques utilizing Gaussian Graphical Models and Bayesian Gaussian Graphical Models. These models utilize the inherent statistical structure present within the data to create a more accurate low-dimensional space. We compared the classification capabilities of these methods across three distinct scRNA-seq datasets, utilizing Bayesian Gaussian Graphical Models for the first time on a public dataset. The results reveal a substantial performance improvement of these methods over Euclidean space methods, with a notable 84% gain on one of the examined datasets. The numerical findings are as follows: a 84% improvement from the SPPC dataset, a 87% improvement from the Pancreas dataset, and a 91% improvement from the Immune Cells dataset. We made these datasets available publicly through our repository, along with the code used to generate these results and create the low-dimensional representations.

The mass distribution of stars within a few parsecs of a supermassive black hole is crucial in determining the scattering rate of stars by these holes. Unlike traditional models, which assume a uniform mass distribution based on a stellar mass function, our research considers the mass function's effect, taking into account stellar masses from 0.1 to 10,000 solar masses, across various regions of a galaxy. By combining this with the proper motions of the Milky Way's center obtained from Hubble Space Telescope data and a realistic representation of a supermassive black hole's gravitational field, our simulations reveal a scattering rate consistent with current estimates, especially for lower-mass stars. However, high-mass star scattering rates exceed predictions. These findings hold significant implications for understanding the observed distribution of star clusters in galaxies and the evolution of a galaxy's core over millions of years.

This work examines the application of Model Predictive Control to systems influenced by uncertainty under minimal assumptions. It's demonstrated that when uncertainty affects the system in a nonlinear manner, MPC can still be effectively implemented. Furthermore, it's shown that uncertainty in the system can be mitigated and, under certain conditions, made progressively smaller. This control strategy is capable of handling a broad range of uncertain systems and can be efficiently realized through specialized hardware.

This research explores the application of compressed sensing techniques to accelerate independent component analysis algorithms. We introduce two novel algorithms, CS-ICA and its enhanced version CS-ICA with the Bayesian method, to efficiently determine the signal mixing matrix in independent component analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms over traditional ICA methods by leveraging a widely used benchmark dataset, the Olivetti faces dataset. Furthermore, our results are compared with the performance achieved using the Fast ICA and JADE algorithms. We found that our compressed ICA algorithms not only significantly reduce memory usage, but also deliver a reasonably accurate separation of mixed signals at a much lower computational cost. We also found that the addition of the Bayesian method enhances the accuracy of our results. Our research opens the door for the application of sensor sharing and deep ICA architectures, which could greatly reduce the necessary resources for operating these algorithms.

The dynamics of an asymmetric noisy voter model with two species, influenced by stochastic events and external noise, are investigated and analyzed. The model's behavior is contrasted with that of a similar system consisting of two species in the late stages of evolution, originating from an initial state of equal populations and identical species. The resulting patterns of species distribution are observed, which include the presence of separate species populations within the system, as well as the dominance of one species over the other. The probability distributions of species outcomes are derived and categorized into different patterns of species competition, where fixed and dynamic species populations coexist. The occurrence of separate species and the survival of both species in the system are assessed in terms of their likelihood of happening. The system's behavior is further analyzed by considering how its characteristics change when various parameters are modified.

Quantum systems' structure is fundamentally linked to their algebraic properties. Ground state representations of von Neumann algebras, which emerge when studying quantum systems' ground states, hold significant importance. We delve into the characteristics of a specific class of von Neumann algebras, known as local algebras, formed by restrictions of site-boson operators' polynomials on frustration-free ground states. Our analysis shows that the local algebra $\mathfrak{B}}\def\ghat{\hat{g}}$ associated with an embedding of boson algebras $\ghat\mathfrak{A}}\def\ghat{\hat{B}}$ and ground state $\rho$ possesses a unique factorization requirement, resulting in a specific classification related to von Neumann algebras. Consequently, the factors arising from this classification possess certain solvable properties. Additionally, the study reveals that the von Neumann algebras employed in quantum field theory, such as those resulting from a quantum gas's canonical representations, belong to this newly classified category of von Neumann algebras. This classification also holds relevance in the context of matrix product operators in condensed matter and quantum optics, providing a potential link between the theory and von Neumann algebras.

We design an advanced quantum system, comprising a coherent feedback loop with two quantum dots and a single photon cavity, in order to study the development and durability of entanglement in the presence of heat. The dynamic behavior of this system is examined using two theoretical methods: series expansion and quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our research indicates that the interaction of heat and coherent feedback can lead to a stable equilibrium temperature difference, even in the absence of light. We also observe the creation of entangled states and their protection against heat through a combination of efficient photon scattering. Notably, the stability of entanglement is significantly enhanced when compared to a system without coherent feedback. The effects of scattering radiation on entanglement are analyzed in detail. Finally, our experiment offers promising prospects for improving the durability of quantum systems, thus advancing quantum information technologies.

We have calculated the one-loop QCD triple-collinear splitting operators and, based on these results, derived the corresponding subtraction terms necessary for infrared divergent mode calculations in sector decomposition. We also verified that all sector decomposition sectors contain a mass and/or collinear divergence, which can be removed by the respective subtraction or counterterm expressions.

Greenberg's strong approximation theorem can be applied to a n-dimensional lattice over a p-adic field by considering (n+1)-dimensional crystals. This connection allows us to extend the range of possible n values, up to n equal to (p-1)/2, according to specific conditions on the lattice. This decision is based on a significant finding from S. Bloch and H. Hansen. By translating this into the context of one-dimensional local rings, we can gain new insights into the range of possible n values, which are then linked back to the original lattice context. This approach helps us confirm a long-standing hypothesis of Kahn, Sieradzki, and Venkatesh. To support this, we also develop an alternative, more streamlined version of Kahn, Sieradzki, and Venkatesh's original proof, which simplifies their argument and removes any reference to the range of n values.

Sundials found in Islamic areas, particularly in Indonesia, hold significant historical value, with their study could provide insight into the region's cultural and scientific past. Although sundials are an important archaeological find, very few comprehensive studies have been conducted on them, and as a result, existing documentation is lacking. To fill this gap, a citizen science approach is proposed that combines the efforts of the public, researchers, and technology to develop an extensive database of sundials. This would involve collecting and compiling data on sundials through collaboration between these groups, utilizing available data such as images, along with visiting and directly observing and recording the sundials themselves. The ultimate goal is to establish a comprehensive database that could aid researchers in classifying and studying sundials, specifically those located in Islamic areas, including those in Indonesia.

A novel hybrid scheme combining TFIET and NFD is proposed to enhance the energy efficiency of DED2D systems. The TFIET-NFD scheme modifies the conventional ZF-CSI channel state feedback process by utilizing pure phase transmission and energy-intensive feedback of narrowband channels, resulting in a hybrid transmission and feedback mechanism. Theoretical analysis indicates that the TFIET-NFD scheme achieves optimal energy efficiency, equals traditional zero forcing feedback in high user density scenarios, and offers improved energy efficiency in comparison to TFIET and traditional zero forcing feedback. Additionally, the scheme has the capability to dynamically adjust the ratio of downlink data and energy transfer power to users. Furthermore, the TFIET-NFD scheme has been optimized for two modes: subchannel per user and multiuser transmission. Optimization results in a 50% increase in energy efficiency in the first mode and a 30% increase in the second mode, in comparison to the existing optimal solution. The TFIET-NFD scheme thus presents an attractive solution for modern wireless networks in scenarios where users require high data rates and energy transfer rates.

The 2020 pandemic has accelerated the shift to remote work and thereby the need for fully automated laboratories to operate round-the-clock to meet increasing experimental demands. Our research focuses on the long-term control of experimental setups, comprising multiple devices, often with limited and irregular scheduling needs. Guided by the principle of minimal human intervention, we set out to uncover the optimal balance between automated laboratory management and timely handling of unexpected incidents or changes. Our proposed approach, the Optimal Long-term Lab Manager (OLLIM), relies on the concept of semi-Markov decision processes to identify the most suitable action for each moment, either automating tasks or delegating them to human experts. Our initial findings indicate that OLLIM is capable of adapting to the specific needs of each laboratory and can significantly reduce the total cost of laboratory management, our primary performance metric. Our practical implementation of OLLIM, utilizing a multi-agent architecture, has successfully demonstrated its effectiveness in a laboratory setting.

We address a conjecture by Asser, which suggests that a specific class of graphs, denoted as $S_2$ and containing all undirected bipartite graphs, exhibits unique intersection properties compared to any single-edge-increased subgraph. While our findings confirm Asser's conjecture for $S_2$, they also reveal a more extensive pattern, showing that for any graph class $C$, $ext{Inter}(C, C+1)$ indeed possesses unique intersection properties. Moreover, this outcome surpasses earlier speculation that even $ext{Inter}(S_2, S_3)$ might not possess this property.

To refine the design of electrostatic phase plates, understand their properties, and ultimately improve the life of high-resolution transmission electron microscopes (HRTEM), various design options for the phase plate are explored. By employing a computational method that maps electron beam trajectories to image plane displacements, the phase plate's properties can be quickly predicted. This approach can utilize either the electrostatic or magnetic fields surrounding the phase plate to deflect electrons. However, due to practical considerations, the computational model initially focuses on the electrostatic phase plate, accounting for the effects of mesh geometry, fill-factor, pixel pattern, and pixel size. The design of the electrostatic phase plate is then optimized using an evolutionary algorithm to minimize a target function, which includes variables representing probe size and current density. The study considers different fill-factors, pixel patterns, and probe sizes to achieve optimal results. The designed electrostatic phase plates show promising characteristics, with the capability to concentrate electron beam current into tiny regions, potentially extending the life of HRTEM microscopes. Additionally, the computational model is adaptable to design magnetic phase plates and can incorporate real-world imperfections to better represent actual system limitations.

An alternative theoretical framework for quantum computation is developed by translating fundamental principles of quantum computation into the language of quantum field theory and revealing the underlying structure of quantum computation through a comparison with other physical mechanisms of computation. The proposed framework is grounded in the fundamental idea that any computational evaluation, whether achieved through quantum computation or otherwise, must be feasible using a limited number of steps. It highlights the distinct role of wave function collapse, measurement, and non-interpretation phases in quantum computation, and shows how the final interpretation phase can be implemented efficiently using a form of classical computation. Moreover, evidence suggests that an exponential number of qubit steps may be required in general to achieve a successful interpretation, despite the possibility of achieving faster non-interpretation phases.

We establish that the number of unique d-dimensional walk positions diverges from the number of unique (d+1)-dimensional walk positions with a constant scaling factor, specifically equal to the product of (d+1) and the total number of negative half-integers less than or equal to d. This finding provides the first instance of a rigorous proof of a central limit theorem for random walk position counts in d dimensions, with counts normalized by the radius.

We're exploring a type of black hole known as a polymer black hole, which is similar to another type of wormhole. Our analysis reveals that this type of hole exists in a 2D space with four spatial dimensions and is characterized by a power-law near the singularity. When the scalar parameter, gamma, is large, the polymer black hole takes on a form that's very similar to a type of wormhole known as the Morris-Thorne wormhole. However, when the scalar parameter is small, the polymer black hole becomes very different from the Morris-Thorne wormhole. Additionally, our research indicates that the energy conditions for this type of black hole are dependent on the spatial coordinates and also on the scalar parameter. As a result, this type of black hole is either incomplete or incomplete with a single point in a spatial slice of a four-dimensional space. Our analysis also reveals that the causal structure of this type of black hole is a type of extension all the way to a finite radius, as observed in a type of wormhole known as the Phrascone wormhole.

Graphene provides an intimate view of the renormalization of its low-energy properties due to electron-electron interaction. By integrating out the electron baths in the Thomas-Fermi theory, we establish a effective single-band model with a velocity defined by renormalization, unlike its undoped counterpart. For doped graphene, this interaction causes a quasiparticle velocity that decreases with doping, resulting in a higher specific heat capacity in comparison to the undoped variant. In the intermediate regime, the interaction's effect shifts from being mildly nonlinear to significantly nonlinear as one moves towards the Dirac point, leading to a reduced velocity and increased specific heat. Additionally, we find that the effective velocity, extracted from the dispersion in the vicinity of the Fermi level, is better represented by its TF-formulation rather than its NA-formulation, especially in the regime of weak doping. Furthermore, the naively expected effective velocity exceeds the TF-formulated velocity, particularly in the regime of weak doping. In contrast, the TF-formulated velocity is superior to the naively expected effective velocity, particularly in the regime of strong doping.

Recent advancements in text-to-speech research are marked by the introduction of MaskedSpeech, a novel approach that fine-tunes large language models using speech-style transformations. These innovations have surpassed top-notch statistical systems in speech synthesis capabilities. However, certain critical elements, such as the ability to produce expressive speech, within acceptable standards of quality and naturalness, remain to be effectively addressed by MaskedSpeech. The limited number of target variables in recent MaskedSpeech systems is considered a hindrance to achieving superior speech synthesis results. The introduction of an additional criterion for optimization, specifically the similarity of generated speech to its unmodified counterpart, has been explored as a possible remedy. The presented study establishes a comprehensive speech synthesis framework, optimized using MaskedSpeech, with an expanded list of target variables and an additional optimality criterion. The results indicate significant and 10% improvement in quality scores and a 16% boost in optimality metrics within this optimized framework.

We address the challenge of incorporating prior knowledge into the variable selection process from Bayesian neural networks by proposing a data-driven approach to refine the posterior distribution of the network's weights and support vectors during the training process. This refinement maintains the original posterior uncertainties and ensures that the selected variables remain consistent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on simulated and real-world datasets, and it is made available through public repositories on GitHub under the CC-BY license.

Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to malicious data manipulation in their input and/or context. Research has focused on generating adversarial examples to compromise DNNs, but little has been done to counter the increasingly common Man-in-the-Middle attacks, which involve modifying both the input and its accompanying metadata. This paper introduces an innovative method to create robust, image-aggressive, Man-in-the-Middle attacks that target DNNs with little overhead, outperforming existing attacks like EAD, and achieving a 99.97% success rate with only 0.42% error rate, at a cost of 0.43% more computational expense compared to a non-robust attack.

According to our analysis of Twitter data, young people's concerns about the
climate change issue are dominated by conspiracy theories rather than scientific
information. The most prevalent conspiracy theories they share relate to the
exaggeration of climate change or artificial control over it, often promoted
by far-right groups. The key group spreading these conspiracy theories are
amateur climate skeptics, using the platform to disseminate unverified
scientific information and thereby undermining established climate knowledge.

The initial findings from the LUX153 dark matter detector have shown that, even with the most sensitive analysis possible, there's still no solid evidence to support the standard model's prediction that dark matter exists. Theoretical models proposing the interaction between dark matter and nucleons are evaluated based on how well they fit with the latest data from direct dark matter detection, taking into account various uncertainties. The implications of cross-validation are also considered, including how well these models align with the results from electric and magnetic monopole searches as well as from dark matter-induced photon scattering experiments.

Building upon Brav and Merling's work on modifying exangulated categories to incorporate Serre duality, we introduce a new concept - 'dualizing triples' - which allows the introduction of Serre duality in exangulated categories. This is represented as a new morphism based on a specific condition, and we demonstrate that its absence is equivalent to the presence of compact objects. Utilizing this framework, we are able to describe the structure of (bounded) dual bases within an exangulated category with Serre duality. Additionally, we use this understanding to characterize bounded dual bases in terms of the existence of Serre duality in subcategories with a particular property.

This study provides a detailed analysis of the financial returns on investment
for various fields of study in Norway and Denmark, employing a detailed data set.
The findings reveal significant disparities in the earnings payoffs to different
fields of study between the two countries, with some fields generating higher
earnings in Norway than in Denmark while others yield higher returns in Denmark.
The data also indicate that differences in earnings payoffs are largely influenced
by variations in the labor market outcomes of different fields of study rather than
by disparities in the level of education as a whole. The findings suggest that
Norway's decentralized vocational system is characterized by lower earnings relative
to Denmark's centralized system. However, Denmark's differences in earnings
payoffs for university and non-university programs are substantially more
pronounced. This study offers policy makers practical information and provides
theoretical underpinnings for recent reforms aimed at enhancing Norway's
vocational education system.

A proposed new generation particle accelerator, called the super $J/ho$ factory, is suggested to be a highly productive research tool for studying various physical phenomena. In addition to serving as an ideal facility for studying the properties of the $J/ho$ particle, this facility could also be utilized to study the characteristics of other excited charmonium states, as well as the production and decay behavior of open charm particles. Furthermore, investigating the characteristics of the $J/ho$ particle at a higher energy range than currently possible, and studying the properties of the $J/ho$ particle in relation to other excited states of the same, are other benefits of this proposal. In order to fully realize the vast potential of this facility, it is suggested that a facility capable of producing collisions at both proton-proton and proton-ion collision energies be developed. In order to meet the requirements of this facility, a comprehensive review of the necessary technical and scientific considerations is undertaken, and a concise overview of this study is presented below.

Our study investigates the accretor-disc dynamics in a two-scale hierarchy system, consisting of a binary at the inner scale interacting with a larger disc formed through the fragmentation of a protoplanetary disc. Utilizing specific numerical setups, we examine how a disc fragment with a mass equal to half that of the binary at its edge interacts with the binary. When compared to a single star of equivalent mass, we find the binary's accretation rate is reduced by half. Additionally, a smaller secondary star leads to a binary-disc equilibrium where the disc's mass is typically less than 10 minus 4 solar masses, consistent with observations of low-mass stars. As the disc fragment grows to equal the binary mass, it migrates inward, leading to a merger within 106 to 108 seconds. During this process, the larger body in the binary either captures or ejects the smaller body, with the disc typically surviving this event. Our findings also suggest disc survival in systems where the smaller body is tossed into an wide orbit, with subsequent binary-hard disc interactions resulting in a variable accretion rate and impact the binary's evolution.

Using the Hubble telescope, researchers obtained highlyprecise measurements of the distribution of dim galaxies at a distance of 9.8 billion light-years. These new data revealed some intriguing findings regarding how matter influences the formation of galaxies and the expansion of the universe. By combining this data with other existing datasets, the researchers conducted a thorough investigation into how matter behaves under gravity within the universe. Their analysis took into account how matter affects large-scale structures across the universe and how it influences the early formation of smaller structures such as galaxies. By modeling these effects, the researchers were able to gain insights into how matter influences the universe and its role in galaxy formation. These new findings revealed that when considering large-scale structures, the speed at which galaxies move and galaxy clusters form is better explained by a model that includes the effects of gravity within these structures. However, when focusing solely on the distribution of galaxies within these structures, the opposite is true. These results suggest that dark matter may still play an important role in understanding the distribution of galaxies within these structures. By combining these new data with existing findings from experiments using light from distant galaxies, the researchers were able to make a precise prediction about how matter behaves under gravity within the universe. These new predictions could inform upcoming experiments with the Hubble telescope and future telescopes, guiding how resources are allocated for projects that involve observing the distribution of dim galaxies using the Hubble telescope.

We present an improved segmentation method for damaged image restoration. A piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model has been widely used for this purpose, but its segmentation performance is limited by its assumption that image regions with different content are separated by sharp boundary lines. We address this limitation by developing a new objective function that not only minimizes the difference between the original and degraded image, but also allows for a smooth degradation of image regions across their shared content. By applying the split Bregman technique to our modified objective function, we are able to derive an efficient algorithm for optimizing this function, and thereby achieve precise image segmentation results even in the presence of significant degradation. Our proposed method successfully demonstrates superior segmentation performance when compared to the conventional Mumford-Shah algorithm and the current state-of-the-art multi-phase image segmentation approach, and its optimized parameter values are automatically derived through an efficiently solved non-convex optimization problem.

The maximum speed limit in ultra-light scalar and vector fields is assessed in terms of field function symmetry. Conversely, no speed limit is imposed on spinors, meaning we can conclude that if dark matter solely comprises ultra-light particles, a sufficient condition is that at least one of the fields either has no speed limit or is a scalar field. Furthermore, it is established that if dark matter is composed of spinors, there is no lower limit on the concentration of these particles in terms of the ultra-light scalar or vector field density. A related finding is that if dark matter is comprised of scalar or vector fields only, a sufficient condition for the complete absence of spinors in dark matter is that the speed limit of these fields is just sufficient to account for the present-day abundance of dark matter. A numerical investigation into the interactions between binary black holes and these ultra-light fields highlights the capability of detecting spinors through gravitational waves, potentially identifying a minimum mass range for these fields, and demonstrates that the speed of these fields must be less than about 0.20c to prevent the complete absence of spinors in dark matter. A related conclusion is that if the speed of these fields is higher than about 0.15c, a sufficient condition for the complete absence of scalar and vector fields in dark matter is that the speed of these fields is just sufficient to account for the present-day abundance of dark matter. Neuromorphic computing holds great promise for delivering unprecedented performance gains in domains such as computer vision and machine learning. On-chip learning is a crucial aspect of neuromorphic systems, which distinguishes it from traditional methods that rely on offline data analysis. In this study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of inductively coupled neuromorphic learning circuits by successfully training a 128x128 photoreceptor array, connected to a 1024-element membrane through 1024 learning elements, with various images from the MNIST dataset. Our results show that neuromorphic learning achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and outperforms previous studies, all of which used fixed weight connections. Additionally, we prove the scalability of our membrane by conducting learning experiments with different circuit configurations, comprising 256 and 512 elements, which demonstrated comparable performance to the 1024-element membrane. Ultimately, we validate the energy efficiency of inductive neuromorphic learning by showing that it consumes significantly less power than a high-performance GPU.

Researchers studied a major noise storm that emerged on AR 2678 near the solar minimum. This intense poloidal event was observed by Parker Solar Probe at 0.16 AU and was found to be a large-scale (approximately 110 Mm in length) sausage mode that traveled at 100-400 km/s and exhibited radiative loss leading to its slow growth. The team interpreted its rapid growth and evolution using theoretical models, a non-uniform hot closed fluxtube and a twisted hot fluxtube. This remarkable event provided valuable insights into the properties and behavior of quiet solar atmosphere.

We developed an innovative design for a compact, flat magneto-optical trap (MOT) using a novel integrated setup, which significantly improved capture efficiency and performance compared to traditional designs. This was achieved through the combination of an integrated ring-shaped dipole trap and a custom planar structure for optical waves, specifically designed to optimize light propagation and trapping effectiveness. The arrangement of the trap and an atomic beam, as well as the positioning of output couplers, enabled efficient interaction between the sample and the output beams, leading to a remarkable 93% efficiency in photon scattering for this novel design - a substantial improvement over previous setups. This integration-driven MOT setup offers significant benefits in terms of system size, complexity, and functionality, and has promising implications for a wide range of applications in quantum technology and quantum sensing.

The powerful jets emanating from supermassive black holes, such as Sgr A* and M87*, have significant implications for our understanding of the co Creation theory. Nonetheless, the source of these jets may be misinterpreted if the black holes are starved of food. This is because the sheared accretion disk, which produces the observed radiation, may not be feeding the black holes as assumed. Instead, the true fuel for these black holes could remain hidden, suggesting the need for a revised approach to the problem.

The goal of this research paper is to examine the modification of photon dispersion caused by the motion of a neutral atom in the presence of a mirror, with particular focus on the distinct case where the atom is undergoing acceleration. The study reveals that when the atom is emotionally detached, the modification of light waves can be represented by a conformal mapping of space-time associated with the covariant form of the conformal group. However, in the absence of the mirror, the known conformal structure of the flat space-time is supplemented by the proper conformal metric, resulting in the celebrated Einstein's equation. Additionally, this paper also explores the concept of deformed photons and explores new applications of deformed Lorentz transformations, all within the theoretical framework of deformed special relativity.

A decade ago, researchers conducted comprehensive studies on the young massive cluster Westerlund 2 using the Hubble Space Telescope, revealing 12 new massive star candidates with a combined total mass of approximately 100 solar masses. These findings suggested a high rate of star ejection from this cluster over the past ten million years, with a efficiency rate comparable to that of the Large Magellanic Cloud. Initially, it was assumed the cluster would eventually lose these stars, but further observations showed that none of these stars had escaped the cluster, instead revealing a surprising state of near-quiescence. Recent discoveries of a pair of star ejection events in this cluster, including the expulsion of a 20 solar mass star still attached to its natal cloud, have now challenged initial assumptions - challenging initial theories that star ejection occurs infrequently and typically happens when a star dies. Contrary to these theories, these new findings suggest that star ejection can occur more frequently, with a higher rate than any other known mechanism.

This research develops a novel approach grounded in the minimax principle, utilizing it to derive new estimates for the minimum and maximum values of functionals in variational problems. By combining this principle with the continuous version of the Fritz John necessary condition, previously proven for finite-dimensional optimization problems in our work, we achieve the extension to infinite-dimensional optimization problems. Our approach is notably independent of specific assumptions concerning the growth of the components of the Lagrange vector, a factor that sets it apart from comparable findings.

To enhance the accuracy of degraded document images, we combine a handwritten text recognizer with a Generative Adversarial Network. However, current text generation models struggle due to limited large-scale handwritten text image datasets. To address this, we utilize the UT-DCIS dataset to develop UT-DCIS-HT, a new dataset containing 123,823 handwritten text image/label pairs by incorporating the UT-DCIS dataset into the UT-CompS dataset, allowing existing models to be replicated on this new dataset. Additionally, we propose a new approach by integrating a handwritten text recognizer with GAN, the Text-to-Image Generation through Recognition (TIGR) method. Through the TIGR approach, given a degraded document, a recognizer produces a text image representation. This representation then acts as the input to a generator, which produces an enhanced image. Recent state-of-the-art text recognition models are limited in their applicability to handwritten text due to being based on pre-trained vision models that prioritize EuroSoFT fonts. To overcome this, we utilize the UT-DCIS-HT dataset to develop the first universal fast text recognizer for handwritten text, outperforming existing models in image-based recognition. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existing text recognizers can be improved by integrating a handwritten text recognizer with the UT-DCIS-HT dataset, specifically the UT-DCIS-HT-SROWD model, which excels over existing models, including the CRNN-AvgPool. The increasing focus on data protection has led to a rise in the importance of extracting specific information from identification documents, such as driver's licenses or national IDs. This process involves not only extracting the required data but also accurately identifying the document type, as there are numerous identification documents with varying structures. Our research aims to explore the effectiveness of deep learning techniques in extracting vital information from ID cards, including document type, name, birth date, gender, ID number, expiration date, and address. To the best of our knowledge, our model achieves record-breaking accuracy on three public datasets, solidifying the efficiency of deep learning methods in this domain. Additionally, we thoroughly evaluate and demonstrates the versatility of our model through an online video and a Python implementation, making our research findings and data accessible to the academic community.

This research focuses on channel estimation for millimeter wave technology, which is set to revolutionize future wireless networks. However, high migration rates significantly hinder channel estimation. To address this challenge, a new approach is proposed, leveraging a long short term memory (LSTM) neural network to enhance estimation resilience in dynamic scenarios. To prepare LSTM for channel estimation, an optimized dataset is created by combining channel simulation with real-world data, ensuring it mirrors the characteristics of actual millimeter wave channels. To fine-tune LSTM, a comprehensive search is conducted, evaluating various parameters. Experimental results show that LSTM-based channel estimation yields a notable 97% improvement in blockage cases and a 58% improvement in general scenarios, compared to a baseline channel estimation model.

We utilize a advanced neural network called a Generative Adversarial Network, commonly
used in the study of images, to improve the quality of astronomical images, specifically
those taken by the Hubble Space Telescope. We frame this as a task called deblurring,
as the network aims to restore a high-resolution image from a lower resolution version.
Our results demonstrate that this method is capable of producing images that are nearly
indistinguishable from real high-resolution images, as judged by experts. We also
determine that neural networks are a promising solution for a range of astronomical
image processing problems.

We examine the limit of our ability to learn simple functions through statistical methods and find that a standard neural network can learn functions with a complexity of e^N, where N is the number of parameters, with high accuracy beyond its training data size, but overfitting can be avoided by using a specific function as a regularizer during training. The regularizer, when applied statically, helps prevent overfitting by restricting the neural network's ability to fit the data beyond its training size. The regularizer can also be applied dynamically during training by incorporating a counterfactual term in the loss function, where the term represents the deviation of the network's prediction from the optimal prediction based on the data's median, and including an optimal counterfactual risk that represents the optimal loss under a fair game. The proposed algorithm, when tested on both the Memorial Best of Three and Double Or Nothing games, demonstrates the ability to learn the optimal strategy beyond its training size without overfitting.

In 2017, the ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel was formally established as a representative of Early Career Researchers within ECFA. Comprised of researchers who started their career within the past ten years, the panel aims to promote Early Career Researcher's interests across European countries. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed various projects such as surveying working and family conditions, gathering input on ECFA's policy matters, and serving as a voice for Early Career Researchers within the federation. This document outlines the panel's initial two-year journey and summarizes its accomplishments, in addition to outlining future goals and aspirations.

Graphical representations in this work illustrate concepts rather than experimental outcomes.
We have developed a basic concept for graphene-based optical identification systems.
Our approach involves graphene patches on gold substrates that support line wave propagation, which can be manual or nano-printed.
This identifies an exclusive platform for graphene's electrical manipulation at the sub-wavelength scale or through near-infrared light, enabling the storage and processing of optical data with compact footprint and high spatial resolution.
Notably, the identified line waves exhibit distinctive characteristics: they are inherently dual-polarized and exist in the form of electrostatic or plasmonic line waves.
Our findings indicate that these line waves can be employed for image processing, akin to classical image processing techniques.
In the near-infrared range, we have demonstrated the practical application of these concepts through the generation of local light patterns that illustrate graphene's capability for optical data manipulation.

This paper presents a Federated Learning framework that enables a network of various agents, comprising human-robot interactions systems, to collaborate and adapt to their shared environment without a centralized authority. By aligning the agents' knowledge and adapting to regional differences, our approach facilitates seamless cooperation. We demonstrate the concept's practical value through a complex search and rescue scenario, where multiple robots and multiple humans work together to search for and respond to incidents across various locations. The framework's effectiveness is showcased through a simulated evaluation, where multiple robots and multiple humans successfully learned to navigate through multiple environments and cooperate to achieve common goals.

This research introduces a new unbiased minimum influence estimator that incorporates a flexible bias correction mechanism. Specifically, our approach leverages the theory of generalized linear models and uses a Gaussian distribution to establish a reference model. The estimator is developed within the framework of influence functions and is demonstrated to be influence function (IF) unbiased. To efficiently estimate its variance in finite samples, our method employs a bootstrap approach. We also propose a pair of unbiased minimum influence estimators based on the Huber loss function, with their corresponding influence functions accurately represented through Taylor expansions. To further address the challenge of smoothing bias in these estimators, we found it practical to apply a kernel smoothing technique on the influence function itself. We found that our estimator compares favorably to the existing bias-reduced estimators in terms of root mean square percentage error (RMS%Error). The theoretical underpinnings of our approach are supported by simulation-based results.

Knowledge graph link prediction aims to identify missing connections between entities. Current approaches incorporate information from relation extraction to predict new relations, yet they fail to consider that extraction data often contains errors. To address this, our study proposes a novel link prediction framework, KRLP-E, which leverages extractions in an unsupervised manner, focusing on accurate predictions. To mitigate errors, we utilize the characteristics of the extraction process to select high-quality information. To prevent overreliance on extraction data, we also develop a graph-based method to incorporate global structural information, ensuring precise predictions. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that KRLP-E outperforms state-of-the-art models, yielding a significant 4% improvement.

These lecture notes review the outcomes of several investigations on the properties of QCD at high density, primarily focusing on the Debye mass in various limit cases. The influence of baryonic chemical potential on the Debye mass across distinct charge types has been determined through a simplified quark-meson model. The results also extend to an approximation of the Debye mass at high baryonic chemical potential for both vector and scalar quark types, and their behavior has been compared.

We investigated the magnetic arrangements within the perovskite family series, Tb3RuO7, Nd3RuO7, and their comparisons with the already known Gd3RuO7. All three compounds exhibit a non-colinear antiferromagnetic configuration but show distinct differences in their magnetic structures. Specifically, the Ru ions within Nd3RuO7 and Tb3RuO7 show varying spins, whereas they exhibit identical spins in the case of Gd3RuO7. Our studies using muon spin rotation and response also revealed unique dynamic effects related to the Rub ions, which further emphasize the complex magnetic arrangements of these compounds.

Our investigation into local function representations within neural networks reveals that they possess an inherent ability to capture the underlying geometry of signals, both within and outside the network's trained manifold. Through our findings, we demonstrate that representations defined by local first-order gradients can effectively map high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional space, thereby enhancing generalization for low-dimensional signals. Additionally, our analysis suggests that the local gradient representation is versatile and can be applied to both classification and regression tasks, as well as situations where data augmentation is employed. We support our theoretical claims with empirical results.

We introduce a novel, semi generative approach that models target variables by leveraging observed data and expert-provided conditional relationships. In contrast to traditional generative models, which aim to capture a variable's natural state and the impact it has on others, our method solely focuses on modeling the target variable, disregarding its potential effects on other, observed variables. A dedicated learning algorithm is developed to incorporate both observed and expert-provided information, and the proposed model is tested on text and network forecasting tasks, outperforming existing methods.

By examining the geometric aspects of deep learning systems, we aim to gain insights into their performance, ultimately allowing us to devise more efficient architectures and training techniques. This study employs geometric analysis to reveal patterns within real-world data sets, as evidenced by the inherent geometry of certain data representations. These findings can be instrumental in designing more effective deep learning frameworks, for instance, by providing a ground zero for neural network design or by guiding the modification of existing algorithms and architectural components. Furthermore, this research may serve as a starting point for a new area of inquiry within geometric deep learning, encouraging the development of novel geometric analysis and processing techniques that can outperform existing methods.

Consider a cubic field of discriminant $d$, obtained as the field obtained from $x^3 - \frac{d}{s^2}$, where the radicand $s$ is either $2$ or $3$. We identify the set of lattice minima for this field and determine the relationships between elements of its $S$-integer basis.

Deep neural networks' (DNNs) intricacy makes them challenging to analyze directly, thus we introduced a novel technique, layerwise relevance propagation, to provide insights into their individual components. By combining this approach with a newly developed relevance framework, we were able to accurately extract relevant variables from real-world data and gain profound insights into DNNs' learning processes. Our research showcases the prediction capabilities of our method on datasets like the ICU patient mortality forecast and the image recognition challenge in fundus disease diagnosis, displaying compelling results. Furthermore, our layerwise relevance propagation allowed us to investigate the decision-making processes of DNNs, thereby contributing to the enhancement of their reliability in critical applications.

Recent research has explored extended versions of important combinatorial objects known as Stirling numbers of the second kind. This study aims to investigate a recently introduced generalization: r-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, initially derived from a modified version of the Lagrange invariant. We will establish a novel, straightforward definition for these generalized Stirling numbers based on a fundamental counting principle, then utilize this definition to express existing recurrence relations for standard Stirling numbers of the second kind in a simplified form. Additionally, a generalized form of the Fletcher-Tseng identity will be derived using this definition.

We introduce a method to visually represent the shape of domains within layered materials by classifying the symmetry of domain walls. This classification allows us to establish a connection between the shape of domains and their surrounding environment. By representing the shape of domains in a structured way, we can study how the size and arrangement of domains change in response to external stimuli. This helps us to gain a deeper understanding of how these materials break down into multiple, self-consistent patterns and how their properties are affected.

We establish that for any Lie group $G$ of dimensions $n$, with its corresponding Lie algebra $ \mathfrak{g}$, the maximum momentum resolution is directly proportional to the deformation parameter $\hbar$ and the geometric diameter of the manifold $G$, with a proportionality constant linked to the universal Riemannian curvature invariant. This outcome is a consequence of our discovery that the number of Casimir operators for a Lie algebra $ \mathfrak{g}$ plays a crucial role in determining the maximum momentum resolution. Additionally, our research reveals that the maximum momentum resolution is linked to the number of Casimir operators and the geometric characteristics of the manifold $G$, allowing us to derive a precise estimate in terms of the Riemannian curvature invariant. We illustrate the validity of our findings through specific examples, including compact Lie groups and specific non-commutative 2-tori.

We introduce an improved variant of the Neural SDE Monte Carlo simulator, incorporating novel elements to enhance efficiency. Firstly, we apply affine coupling layers utilizing matrix-valued affine transformations for greater effectiveness in normalizing simulated outcomes. Secondly, we substitute complex-valued parameters in these coupling layers to expedite simulations by reducing a factor of two through the use of faster, single precision arithmetic. Lastly, we address a persistent bias in the conventional NSDE approach and incorporate a correction technique to guarantee precise results for all simulation time intervals. Our enhanced NSDE model, named NVSDE, surpasses the conventional NSDE in both speed and precision, with our results demonstrating substantial quantitative gains.

We propose a model incorporating $\text{SU}(3)_C\times \text{U}(1)_F\time \text{U}(1)_B\time \text{U}(1)_X$ as its symmetry group, where unique symmetry breaking patterns are employed to explain the disparate quark masses within the third generation. Specifically, the breaking of $\text{U}(1)_F$ and $\text{U}(1)_X$ symmetries contribute to generating a large top-bottom mass split. Furthermore, we identify a mode in the scalar potential that facilitates $\text{SU}(3)_C$ breaking without inducing too-late electroweak symmetry breaking (EWBS). Lastly, we analyze flavor violations arising from the $\not{M}_3$ matrix and find that they align with the observed hierarchy among the top, bottom, and strange quark masses.

Our investigation into recently emerged Virtual Performance Monitoring Points reveals that existing protection methods are ineffective against sophisticated attacks utilizing VPPMs, and that current research has overlooked the implementation of reliable VPPM security measures. In light of this, we aim to contribute to the advancement of VPPM security by exploring the possibilities and necessities of VPPM protection. By examining the inherent characteristics of VPPMs, the pronounced risks associated with their exploitation are identified. Furthermore, a comprehensive framework for VPPM security is developed, along with an outline of the specific security measures that can be incorporated within virtualization platforms to prevent and mitigate the malicious utilization of VPPMs. In the context of cloud computing, the importance of transparent and timely notification to the cloud tenant on suspected VPPM malicious activity is emphasized. The challenges and potential avenues for further research in this area are also discussed.

Language models are increasingly being used across diverse languages to various effects.
Our research builds on this trend, exploring the adaptability of these models with
minimal data, specifically targeting non-English languages. We discovered that such
adaptability heavily relies on the training of the underlying language model, while
factorizing the adaptability into two distinct aspects - vocabulary and structure -
has shown great potential in guiding language-industries towards sustainable,
long-term development. Additionally, our work highlights the significance of weight
sharing and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in enhancing adaptability.

Research has shown that rotating core collapse begins with rotating cores having roughly equal masses of binary systems, with the ratio of their kinetic energy to gravitational energy increasing as these cores form protostars.  However, it's been observed that this ratio in these developing binary systems follows an irregular pattern, as observed in a collection of simulated rotating core collapses where the ratio varies significantly.  To clarify the results from these simulations, an analysis was conducted to compare the physical properties of these developing binary systems, including their mass, angular velocity, and physical characteristics.  It was discovered that the mass of these developing binary systems is directly correlated with their kinetic energy in relation to their gravitational energy, and that the kinetic energy in these systems is regulated by their individual mass and velocity.  In order to better understand the potential potential end-products of these rotating core collapses, an analysis was conducted to compare the results from these simulations with actual data collected from real systems, including the binary system system that formed in a collection of rotating cores that had a mass range of approximately $1.4 \odot M$ to $2.0 \odot M$.  In contrast to actual data collected from real systems, it was discovered that the ratio of kinetic energy to gravitational energy in the systems studied was significantly lower, and that the mass of these developing binary systems was not a determining factor in their kinetic energy. The construction of the m-ar-K function in the infinite dimensional Hilbert space equips a data set with a more refined structure, enabling a more effective dimensionality reduction than what can be achieved through traditional methods. Building upon this foundational concept, the m-ar-K function is adapted for use in the Euclidean space, where its application has been limited to data sets of dimensionality three or higher. In this research, the Euclidean m-ar-K function is further developed by introducing a simplified, computationally efficient formula that makes the algorithm's implementation more practical. In addition to introducing this new formula, the article's final section demonstrates the benefits of using the Euclidean m-ar-K function through a series of numerical experiments that compare its performance against other relevant techniques.

A recent breakthrough in circuit evaluation has given rise to renewed speculation over the computational complexity of the Turing machine's fundamental operation, defined by a certain class (EPC). A significant non-polynomial time lower bound for EPC could imply that PTIME does not necessarily contain its dual, COMP. This possibility suggests that PTIME and COMP may not have a clearly defined relationship. Moreover, a super-polynomial time lower bound for EPC may further shed light on the fundamental operation of the Turing machine. It's interesting to note that even without resolving the P!= NP question, a super-polynomial time lower bound for EPC would allow us to precisely define the differences between several complexity classes, including a notable one (F_2) and its dual (F_t). In circuit evaluation, a pivotal role is played by a two-player game where the first player aims to win an election by distributing votes among several candidates. The interacting Turing machine model, first introduced by Chor et al., appears to be the perfect framework for studying fundamental operations of the Turing machine. It's specifically the model where the first player executes a polynomial number of steps and interacts with a simulator performing a super-polynomial number of steps to develop a super-polynomial time lower bound for EPC. In the interacting Turing machine model, the first player aims to win an election by efficiently distributing votes among a super-polynomial number of candidates after a polynomial number of interactions with the simulator.
