By utilizing these data sets, researchers can investigate various scales of turbulence, from large distances to individual Debye lengths, providing new insights into the solar wind.

To investigate the impact of real-world oscillator amplitude fluctuations and 
different chirp-taper schemes on undulator-based X-ray free-electron lasers (FELs), 
we conducted detailed simulations. Our study specifically focused on the effects 
of varying chirp and oscillator amplitude at different gain media positions. 
Results showed that implementing a proper chirp-taper scheme, even with significant 
fluctuations, can still enable the creation of ultra-short pulses in certain 
configurations. However, if no chirp-taper is applied and the oscillator has 
significant amplitude fluctuations, the resulting pulse can experience a critical 
delay, leading to a significant increase in pulse duration and poor pulse 
coherence. In addition, our research explored the interplay of pure Landau instability 
and gain narrowing at different gain media positions, highlighting their distinct 
properties. These findings contribute to improving our understanding of oscillator 
seeding schemes for FELs and can inform the development of practical oscillator 
seeding techniques.

We analyze the vertical velocity perturbations, $w$, under the assumption that the geostrophic approximation holds in the atmosphere. By incorporating the Boussinesq approximation, we derive a modified Taylor-Goldstein equation. This equation differs from its classical counterpart, which is obtained under the usual hydrodynamic approximation when $w$ is small. We demonstrate that even though $w$ is relatively small, its contribution can lead to significant variations in the equilibrium mean flow. This emphasizes the importance of using the geostrophic approximation in conjunction with the Boussinesq approximation to study atmospheric vertical velocity perturbations.

Closely contested local elections often hinge on a candidate's districting strategy, at which point analysts and experts seek to assess the fairness of the chosen plan. To address this, we've developed an open-source tool utilizing Simulated Annealing to evaluate the strategic equivalence of districting maps. This method, which relies on a graph representation, applies a range of local transformations to mimic natural annealing, aiming to find optimal equivalence configurations. By combining Simulated Annealing with a fairness assessment metric, we're able to determine the fairness of a given districting plan. To compare our approach with existing tools, we've applied our method to a set of known districting plans in the state of Maryland.

A novel and efficient method is proposed to enhance fabric defect detection by separating and extracting defects from the given fabric image background using low-rank decomposition. This method first divides the fabric image into several blocks and calculates the background block-by-block. Each block is then subjected to low-rank decomposition based on its clean representation, allowing for the effective separation of defect information. An optimal segmentation approach is subsequently employed to accurately identify and effectively work on each defect. Finally, the segmentated areas are least-squares regressed to obtain the ultimate defect map. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the robustness and superiority of the proposed method in terms of generalization ability and effectiveness. Furthermore, a corresponding algorithm has been successfully applied to the FDDB2018 benchmark, achieving remarkable performance with an area under the curve (AUC) of $95.95\%$ for rotation invariance and $98.95\%$ for fixed angles.

Optimizing an agent's performance in various tasks often requires balancing new sensory input with existing knowledge. This is achieved by selecting actions that are informative enough to merit taking, while also considering the value of retaining existing observations. In our research, we establish a baseline policy for agents to follow by identifying the most informative actions by leveraging the mutual information between actions and observations. This mutual information is calculated through a novel, straightforward approach employing a mutual information network (MIN) and a variational information bottleneck (VIB) setup. In experiments, we found that our method yielded consistently high rewards in a range of tasks, including an evaluation environment where an agent had to collect a set of objects while navigating a room. Notably, our approach even performed better than a comparison agent in an evaluation study, and we propose possible future improvements to navigate more complex environments.

We've found that in the Brans-Dicke theory, a certain type of gravitational wave, assuming certain properties, will always be detected by observers far enough away, and this is consistent with the theory's own predictions. Moreover, we've demonstrated that photons traveling through the scalar gravitational field of a collapsing star must pass through a critical point before reaching infinity, and this is supported by the theory. Using the properties of geodesic deviation, we've been able to describe the scalar gravitational wave's behavior in the vicinity of this critical point.

We have developed a numerical framework to simulate the formation and evolution of the first binary systems in the universe's history, consisting of stars born from the merger of two primordial objects. Our approach uses a hydrodynamical simulation of 37 microparsecs on a side, which we've expanded upon, to model the merger of 64 initial binary systems based on certain criteria. Our results show that the rate at which these binary systems merge peaks around z ≈ 20 with an estimated count of 0.43 year to the power of -1 gigaparsec to the power of 3. To improve precision, we plan to increase the scale of our simulation to 377 microparsecs and model up to 614 initial binary systems in the future.

Incident detection in modern distribution networks with various advanced devices poses significant challenges, and traditional methods are often inadequate. In response, researchers have explored data-driven approaches for incident detection and prediction frameworks. This research builds on their work by developing a novel incident detection and prediction framework based on a reduced-order model that is specific to distribution networks. Notably, this framework can accommodate and model various distribution grid structures, including series and parallel connections of energy storage systems, and is trained using real-time monitoring data. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation-based validation, where a simplified model of a distribution grid with series and parallel connections and real-time monitoring data are used to detect incidents with high accuracy.

The hadronic decay X(3872) to J/psi pi pi gamma is studied in the context of low energy QCD using chiral U(3) symmetry. A specific effective Lagrangian is presented to describe the various mesonic contributions. Through a straightforward calculation, the branching ratios for several decay channels are determined. Notably, the calculated contributions of the rho and omega mesons significantly outnumber those of other mesons. Additionally, the calculated width for the decay X(3872) to J/psi pi gamma is presented.

This overview provides a thorough introduction to the classification of smooth quadrics within a specific dimension, based on their defining matrices, as well as their geometric representations, offering a detailed look at how these classifications intersect with other areas of study in arithmetic geometry.

We introduce TextWorldExpress, a simulated text-based game platform designed to enhance the development and research of text-based games and learning methods. TextWorldExpress reframes the process of creating and running text-based games into data-driven experiments. This new approach combines the capabilities of two powerful tools, TextWorld and Jupyter, to streamline the collection and analysis of qualitative and quantitative data throughout the game simulation process. With TextWorldExpress, developers can create custom text-based games and run experiments using their existing collections of Game Description Languages. Our enhanced platform includes automated data analysis capabilities, enabling researchers to compare outcomes with historically conducted studies. Furthermore, TextWorldExpress accommodates two novel analysis techniques: the calculation of a new metric for evaluating simulation throughput and qualitative assessment of agent performance. To illustrate the functionality of our platform, we present a case study investigating the effectiveness of current state-of-the-art agent architectures using our experimental framework. With TextWorldExpress, researchers can efficiently conduct comparative studies of different agent architectures to inform the development of more effective textual models.

Three-dimensional Topological Insulators exhibit protected surface electron circulation that can be influenced by external influences like vibrations and imperfections. In the event that these imperfections reach the surface, they can significantly impact the electron propagation, potentially trapping it in closed loops as a result. This research focuses on the electron response to dislocation imperfections within 3D Topological Insulators. A theoretical framework is developed to analyze the electron interaction with these defects, and the associated energy changes are calculated, revealing various energy shift patterns based on the type of vibration and core edge pass-through. An interesting core effect emerges, where certain vibration types lead to the elimination of electron backscatter at the dislocation core. A simulation model illustrating the electron circulation patterns in the presence of dislocations is introduced, and the associated electron circulation behavior is examined under different vibration conditions. An interesting finding shows that certain vibration types can induce a smooth, continuous electron circulation without any disruption at the dislocation core. An interesting core effect emerges, where certain vibration types lead to the elimination of electron backscatter at the dislocation core.

The research explores $p$-harmonic functions within specific domains and their behavior at boundary points. We verify the uniqueness of these functions under certain conditions, depending on the value of $p$. The study also provides information about the functions that satisfy these conditions. We find that increasing $p$ enhances uniqueness, a finding related to the properties of convex domains. The investigation extends to nearly convex domains, bringing together concepts from geometry and analysis.

By utilizing the Max-stable process concept from spatial statistics, we develop a model to describe and analyze extreme weather patterns on a global scale. This is based on data from the Metop satellite, which measures wind speed, wind wave height, and significant wave period. We focus on developing a practical and intuitive max-stable model for extreme wind speed and wave height by averaging the wind speed and wave height fields over large areas, such as 1000x1000km, and then maximizing these averages for events in the top 1% of the wind speed distribution. We find that significant wave period behaves differently and is not well captured by this approach. We apply our model to analyze the spatial relationships between extreme weather patterns and as a tool to investigate multi-model ensemble results from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast, which shows a maximum extent of about 1000 to 1300km of extreme weather patterns that need to be independent. We find that there is an overlap in the areas where we can find multiple Metop wind speed extremes and Metop wave height extremes, which suggests that there is a common factor and these weather patterns are related. We also find that there is an area where Metop wind speed extremes can affect future weather patterns, which suggests a potential link, and that this impact can be seen up to 24 hours in the forecast.

We provide an alternative proof that hyperbolicity of a variety implies the existence of a non-degenerate rational curve. This curve's parameter space is hyperbolic as well. While the original proof by Guedj and Kobayashi focused on the complex setting, our approach works in any complete ground field of characteristic zero. We build on previous efforts by Piroux and our recent publication with Tynela, expanding its applications here.

We've developed a novel geometric framework to interpret manipulability matrices and ellipsoids within the context of Riemannian manifolds. By doing so, our analysis uncovers the underlying Riemannian structure as the natural framework for understanding manipulability. We then use this insight to introduce a new geometric approach to optimizing manipulability. This method is inspired by the ellipsoidal method but is based on a distinct set of coordinates. The resulting algorithm enables the calculation of task-space velocities without direct joint-space manipulation, a capability that may hold significant practical value.

Theoretical predictions for top quark pair production in association with Higgs boson production have been reviewed, specifically at the LHC with emphasis on its impact on Higgs boson detection. Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods are used to generate theoretical predictions along with a likelihood fit to guide the analysis of potential detector-level signatures at the LHC. This includes top quark pair production with an additional bottom quark, a scenario where the Higgs boson can be identified through its decay into bottom quark pairs or pairs of gamma rays. A quantitative evaluation of the Higgs boson signal contribution by the top quark pair process to the detection of Higgs boson signals in experiments is provided. Additionally, the prospects for detecting the top quark pair process at the High-Luminosity LHC have been evaluated based on the expected performance of the ATLAS and CMS experiments. Finally, the prospects for detecting the top quark pair process at future hadron colliders, specifically the FCC-hh, have been assessed.

Our research proposes an efficient, multi-stage training method that is both straightforward and logical to implement. This method addresses the difficulty in teaching 3D object estimation models to recognize canonical poses. To overcome this challenge, we have developed a training process where the models first learn generic features, then receive additional training on pose-specific data, utilizing real-world images. Our method's results demonstrate improvement in both canonical pose learning and overall 3D object estimation capabilities, in comparison to existing techniques. Additionally, our unique dataset consisting of real-world images, denoted as PINOCCHI, includes both cyborg-style categories and implicit poses, making it an ideal resource for testing our multi-stage training process. Our method has been successfully applied to the public dataset, KITTI, as well as our developed dataset, PINOCCHI, to test its efficacy.

The widespread problem of vaccine-related misinformation has significant real-world consequences, leading to a lack of informed opinions on immunization. To address this, we introduced a framework that combines large amounts of social media data with sophisticated analytical tools to grasp users' attitudes towards such misinformation. Our framework employs BERT-based text analysis and graph neural networks to measure the impact of vaccine-related misinformation on public opinion, considering multiple factors including perception, sentiment, and graph structure. Our analysis of Twitter data reveals important insights into the relationship between linguistic and graphical characteristics, demonstrating that both are crucial to understanding users' attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation.

The ability to control the central energy and temporal duration of attosection pulses generated via high-harmonic generation, primarily through modification of laser parameters, is limited. Our research introduces a novel technique to independently regulate the pulse energy and duration by incorporating a neutral atom interacting with the fundamental field. The harvested attosection pulses show a notable shift in energy and a few-femtosecond change in temporal duration. The underlying physical process can be utilized to manipulate extreme ultraviolet pulses and offer insights into the intricate interactions between matter and light.

We've been monitoring the bright eclipsing binary system Algol C (Beta Persei) for over 160 years, and our recent findings, based on a comprehensive data set spanning from 1876 to the present day, reveal no significant changes in its orbital period. Our research using advanced photometry and spectroscopy has also uncovered intriguing patterns, including subtle color changes and spectral variations, which suggest the presence of circumstellar dust. Additionally, our analysis indicates that Algol C's secondary star is most likely a giant G-dwarf star with approximately 5.5 solar masses.

We provide an example that shows the absence of bound on a specific solution of the Cauchy problem for the Schrödinger equation in a specific domain under given constraints. This solution behaves badly near the boundary of the domain. The properties of this solution are similar to those found in a previous study, except the boundary conditions are different. The approach used to obtain this result involves changing the context from a real space to a complex space and then using a specific transformation to obtain the solution. The properties of this solution can be obtained by using a particular operator and lemma.

Deep Neural Networks (DNN) have become an essential part of solving inverse problems, and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have been considered a breakthrough in solving high-resolution inverse problems with a minimal number of measurements. However, PINNs training can be a computationally expensive task, requiring a significant amount of time. To overcome this limitation, a new approach is presented that utilizes expert knowledge to sample data points more efficiently. A residual-based adaptive node generation method is introduced, initially estimating data points based on expert knowledge and then refining them incrementally during the training process. To optimize data points, they are grouped into two categories: input and output data points. Input data points are generated based on expert knowledge, and output data points are derived from these input data points using a discriminator network. A new loss function, known as the Pythagorean constraint, is introduced and combined with the initial PINNs loss function. Experimental results on solving inverse problems under different scenarios demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, and the comparison with existing methods, such as PINNs and the Expert-Knowledge-Guided PINNs, demonstrates its superiority.

This research focuses on the unique properties of ferroelectric gate metal-oxide-semiconductor transistors (FeFETs), incorporating a polar ferroelectric film, by examining the boundary between two domains with opposite polarization charges. By investigating the spatial distribution of charges across this boundary, we develop an understanding of the influence of domain walls on the conduction band profile and the behavior of electrons. By leveraging the domain periodicity and the stability of charges, we reveal the existence of a stable electron cloud at the boundary between domains, facilitating the manipulation of electrons and enabling the precise tuning of semiconductor properties, thereby potentially enhancing FeFET performance and efficiency.

We have developed a portfolio of techniques to tackle the challenge of Cargo library dependency vulnerability management. Since 2015, our proposed methods have been shared with the Cargo community and have guided the development of Cargo's built-in vulnerability checker. These techniques and their implementation as a vulnerability database have helped provide reliable vulnerability information to thousands of developers and have guided the development of Cargo's built-in vulnerability checker. Our techniques and the shared database have also empowered the Rust community to make informed choices and enabled successful integration of vulnerability information into popular code review platforms and version control systems. Currently, our database contains vulnerability information for over 78 thousand Cargo packages, which reveal disturbing facts: more than 7 in 10 libraries are still vulnerable in their latest versions, while around 4 in 10 are still vulnerable even when using the latest secure versions of their dependencies. Our analysis also shows that a significant majority of libraries are still using outdated and vulnerable versions of dependencies, which highlight the importance of carefully managing library versions in the Rust ecosystem. Our database and analysis provide insight into the challenges of library version management in the Rust ecosystem and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed techniques in addressing these challenges.

This research investigates the ergodic properties of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations, driven by various types of noise, in a two-dimensional domain. Both jump and continuous noise scenarios are examined. In the presence of jump noise, a pure jump equivalent model is introduced, and ergodicity is established, along with a key finding that finite exponential moments can be guaranteed. For noise consisting of a combination of continuous and jump components, conditions are identified that ensure ergodicity can be proven. These results are supported by a range of numerical simulations.

For any finite non-cyclic abelian group G, the power graph G^n is defined with edges connecting elements that have one as their greatest common divisor. The minimum degree of this power graph, d_n(G), is determined by the number of edges incident on each element, considering the order of G and n greater than or equal to 2. The elements of order e in G form a spanning subgraph with degree n-1, while elements of order greater than e have a potential degree of n, and those in the torsion-free nilpotent subgroup have a degree of 1, as they only connect to the identity element. The degree of a non-cyclic abelian group is at most 2 for n = 2, at most 3 for n = 3, and at most 2 plus a prime number p greater than 3 for n = p. The degree of a non-cyclic abelian group is completely defined by the order of its elements and the smallest prime number p that divides the order of G, where the order of its elements is the least common multiple of p and another number t, with the exception when p is 2, in which case the degree is at most 5, and when both p and t are 2, in which case the degree is at most 3.

The energy reach of the Large Hadron Collider at 6.5 TeV per nucleon-nucleon pair has surpassed the 1970s experiments at the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings, which reached an energy of 24 GeV per nucleon-nucleon pair. To investigate how particle production varies with increasing energy, we developed a special data set from the CERES experiment at the LHC, which was carried out in parallel with a specific detection system. This was done by analyzing only a limited number of charged particles and considering specific acceptance criteria. After doing this, we found that results from the CERES and NA49 experiments at the CERN proton synchrotron, which operated at lower energy, show consistent patterns. These findings also align with predictions from perturbative QCD and other theories.

Recent research has shown that Gabor filters, specifically Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), offer a robust solution for image representation. LGFs are well-suited for semantic tasks such as classification and semantic segmentation. However, existing work has focused on the correlation of LGFs with specific image features (e.g., edges, corners, etc.), without fully exploring the potential contributions of multiple Gabor kernels for a more effective image representation. To address this limitation, this study proposes a new approach, the Linear Combination of Gabor Kernels (LCK), which aims to combine multiple Gabor kernels to improve the robustness of image representation. The LCK method utilizes an LSTM-based network to learn and adapt the weights of Gabor kernels for various tasks and conditions. The efficacy of LCK is demonstrated on classification and semantic segmentation tasks within the ImageNet dataset, where LCK outperforms baseline models by 10 and 13 percentage points.

Graph Convolutional Networks are highly effective at addressing graph-related issues, yet their intricate structure makes them difficult to modify and comprehend. Despite numerous enhancements to GCNs, understanding how individual components impact performance remains obscure. We investigate the core mechanics of GCN by utilizing rigorous theoretical analysis, which reveals how graph feature gathering and aggregation influence the final outcome. By executing a comprehensive set of experiments, our findings conclude that rearranging the order of feature gathering has a noticeable impact on training and validation results, while also accelerating computation.

Advanced neural network security is under scrutiny due to the emergence of sophisticated attacks, such as adversarial trojans. Our research introduces an improved adversarial trojan attack with enhanced stealth and applicability. The traditional generative adversarial network, which relies on text representations, is inefficient in real-world scenarios. Our enhancement is a dual-encoder framework that directly utilizes image features, allowing our trojanized neural network to be trained on a smaller, uncorrupted dataset. Our novel attack includes two key components: first, generating a minimal and category-specific image trigger using our encoder; second, maximizing the disturbance caused by this trigger. Our study includes quantitative evaluations of our proposed attack, including successful infiltration and data corruption tests, which demonstrate its superior adaptability and applicability in real-world scenarios. Our analysis further reveals that our trigger is distinct and minimally obstructive. Our research also introduces an effective detection methodology to counter our proposed attack, which relies on trigger detection. Our study validates the efficacy of our proposed detection method, preventing data corruption and model infiltration.

The introduction of the ROSIE IFU, featuring its unique 2D BBs 40 and its capabilities for low-resolution spectral mapping across 1300 to 5400 Angstroms with 7.13 Angstroms resolution, significantly expands the system's coverage to 40 by 40 spatial pixels. This upgrade significantly boosts the area that can be mapped in comparison to previous IFU, allowing for full-band observations of large objects such as nebulae and galaxies in significantly less time. The Rosie IFU, paired with the IFU's reimagining of BBs as smaller, more versatile areas, can now efficiently perform extensive mapping tasks across a broad range of objects. We outline the IFU's reimagined observational parameters, detailing changed and retained features, and provide guidance on classifying observed objects utilizing standardized spectroscopic astronomical nomenclature. We discuss the IFU's reimagined extensive mapping parameters, including various ppx sizes, and illustrate their effects on a diverse set of objects. Furthermore, we provide a suggested hierarchy for prioritizing the IFU's reimagined extensive mapping parameter sets.

This review focuses on the current research and recent findings regarding low-energy astrophysical S-factors, essential for understanding how stars fuse nuclei to maintain stability. It includes an overview of experimental and computational methods, specific highlights from recent measurements and paper discussions, an examination of key trends and patterns, and concludes by exploring potential future directions for research in the field.

Recent discoveries of small, temperate exoplanets, referred to as exo-Earths, have generated significant interest in their study. Studies of these planets revolve around the sun-like star TOI-2065 and an Earth similar planet, TOI-2065 e, in particular. TOI-2065 e stands out due to its suitable climate and mineral composition, making it an ideal candidate for examining Earth-like systems. Employing periodogram and correlation analysis on light curve data, researchers analyzed the structural and atmospheric characteristics of TOI-2065 e. Utilizing planetary interior simulation models, they further investigated the planet's internal structure. Interestingly, while static models reveal similar mineral compositions to those of Earth, dynamic simulations reveal differences in TOI-2065 e's interior. Notably, the planet is more prone to dynamic activity, with potential effects on its atmosphere and temperature, which may be less similar to those of Earth.

This research focuses on developing a novel neural network that incorporates
up-to-date channel information to enhance performance in complex systems. By
utilizing available pilot data, the proposed NetCSI is designed to capture
variations in channel state and incorporate important aspects. By incorporating
this information, the model achieves improved results on existing datasets.

We introduce a new framework for modal logic semantics using the concepts of topological categories. This framework allows for the incorporation of various logical semantics, including both classical and intuitionistic versions with or without quantifiers. By employing topological categories, we develop a general method for modeling logical semantics, and subsequently, construct a new class of Kripke models. This approach provides a fresh perspective on existing Kripke models and, through the use of topological categories, offers a more unified understanding of the underlying semantics.

We offer an evidence for the 1990 hypothesis proposed by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza, claiming that every bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3 can be colored with a maximum of 4 edge colors in a strong manner.

For various choices of n, i, j, and q, the minimum degree of a function's support within the eigenspace of the graph G_{n,q} associated with the Hamming graph H_{n,q} is investigated. Specifically, it has been demonstrated that $\Delta(G_{n,q})$ equals $n-\lceil\log_2(j+i)\rceil$ whenever $j+i$ is less than $2^{n-1}$, and it has been shown that the opposite scenario is characterized by a function that is constant on one of the two cosets of the permutation group $S_n/I_{n,j+i}$ within the eigenspace. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the opposite scenario is characterized by a function that is constant on one of the two cosets of the permutation group $S_n/I_{n,j+i}$ within the eigenspace.

COPASI is a widely-used biochemical networks simulator and analyzer, accessible through a dedicated application. This has previously been integrated with SBML, widening its compatibility with other software. This integration, however, was limited to importing models, not allowing for the creation or modification of new models within the original application. This integration has now been further expanded with ShinyCOPASI, a web-based interface that not only facilitates the import and export of models, but also allows for the creation and modification of new models, providing a means to interact with COPASI models beyond the standalone application. ShinyCOPASI serves as a backend for online services such as BioModels, allowing for the integration with BioPAX through SBML conversions.

This review article presents an in-depth analysis of various techniques used to tackle inverse and ill-posed problems through the utilization of deep learning-based neural networks. While traditional methods for solving such problems often rely on regularization techniques such as Tikhonov, Morozov, and Tretiakov, deep learning has emerged as a more effective approach, albeit often characterized by a lack of transparency due to its reliance on highly non-linear components such as ReLU and sigmoid functions. The article seeks to explore the potential of combining regularizations and data-driven methodologies in neural networks, with a special focus on the importance of overfitting and its implications for solving ill-posed problems, with real-world applications in imaging techniques such as tomography and compressive sensing.

We identify the conditions under which the class function algebra of certain quantum groups is a maximal abelian self-adjoint algebra. Our analysis covers a range of quantum groups, beginning with $SU_q(2)$ where existing methods fail, and continues with $SU_q(n)$, $U_q(n)$, and $GL_q(n)$. Furthermore, the integrability of central functions within the non-commutative case of $SU_q(2)$ is demonstrated.

We develop a straightforward adaptation of inexact George's Minimum Research Ensemble (GMRES) method for policy iteration in a large-scale Markov decision process. This implementation takes advantage of the Krylov subspace approximation already employed by GMRES. By combining the constraints of non-negative returns and suboptimality bounds with GMRES's residual minimization, we create a convergent iterative process. The computational efficiency of inexact GMRES policy iteration (IGMRESPI) is demonstrated through our analysis and experiments. Specifically, a large MDP with 10,000 states shows IGMRESPI converges 5-7 times faster than traditional policy iteration. The code for IGMRESPI is available on our repository.

Consider a weighted oriented graph, G, and the edge ideal, I, derived from it. Defined is a symbolic power of I, denoted by I^s, where s represents a vector of nonnegative integers. We investigate the relationship between ordinary and symbolic powers of I, specifically when I is the edge ideal of a weighted oriented tree, or d-orientable weighted oriented graph. We establish a equality, s+t = t', which defines a monomial ideal, or 'quasy G-monomial ideal', as a new concept, and explore the properties and implications of this concept. It is also shown that for a weighted oriented graph, G, and edge ideal, I, the equality of ordinary and symbolic powers of I can be represented as a consequence of a quasy G-monomial ideal, or 'qG-mi', having a certain nilpotent property.

This study offers a practical and efficient approach to evaluating inverse problems on realistic scenarios by optimizing a real-world computer simulator. In our experiment, we focused on the inverse weak-scattering problem in the context of X-ray transmission imaging. Our approach distinguched from existing methods in several key ways: first, we did not assume that the true scattering profile was smooth or sparse; second, we employed iterative data-driven optimization without any prior knowledge; and third, we utilized our originally developed optimization tool, an efficient and accurate computer simulator, to recreate real-world conditions and enhance generalization and robustness. Our results indicated the feasibility and efficiency of our approach, and we believe that refining our computer simulator and optimizing other parameters could lead to groundbreaking improvements in imaging technology. This study was conducted as the first step in a two-part project, with the second phase set to utilize machine-learning techniques to enhance our computer simulator and develop a more robust and generalized solution for the inverse-scattering problem.

This research investigates the principles of fair learning under data perturbations within various statistical models, applying these concepts to an 'all-or-nothing' learning framework where an algorithm seeks to determine if a given point falls within a specified half-space. Fair learning is achieved by banning 'extreme' decisions on the part of the algorithm. Our work has two key components: Firstly, we establish the influence of the query radius and concept class on the fairness of all-or-nothing learning under different data perturbations. Secondly, we find that robust fairness is possible in certain concept classes such as linear functions in high dimensions but cannot be accomplished in other classes like monotone convex functions.

This study undertakes a comprehensive examination of how the presence of an isolated photon affects the behaviour of other particles, particularly their distribution and momentum, immediately after a high-energy collision. Research focused on understanding this phenomenon, known as a photon-associated jet, has been conducted using the Vincia event generator to create simulated data and compare against real-world observations from the LHC. Our analysis concentrates on how the presence of the photon impacts the behaviour of other particles, particularly their distribution and momentum, immediately after a high-energy collision. Our findings highlight significant discrepancies between the event generator's predictions and actual measurements, suggesting the need for improved event generators to describe this complex phenomenon.

This study examines the evaluation of Apéry-type series in relation to multiple zeta values, considering both alternating and non-altering versions. While the non-altering version is found to have solutions involving colored multiple zeta values with a specific level, the alternating version is shown to have a more complex solution requiring colored multiple zeta values with an increased level.

Precise characterization of distant or moving objects, such as brown dwarfs, relies on combining multiple measurements, including those of position, velocity, and parallax, as well as a reliable model of their light emission. Recent advancements in spectroscopic photography using the Palomar High-precision Parallax-velocity Survey (PHPPS) have allowed for simultaneous measurement of velocity, metallicity, and temperature of brown dwarfs through analysis of their near-infrared spectra. This, combined with other data, has enabled the development of a reliable model of photometry and the determination of a reliable distance, as well as allow for the identification of moving brown dwarfs. This research applies a Bayesian method to analyze data from multiple sources and utilize the motion of these objects, as well as p-value information to verify the consistency of observational data with theoretical models. Our results indicate that, in many cases, there is less than a 4% chance that the object's spectrum does not match a theoretical model derived from its temperature and metallicity analysis.

These proceedings summarize findings from recent LHC experiments regarding high-energy particle collisions, specifically focusing on measurements obtained from lead-lead, proton-proton, and proton-lead interactions at energies of 5.02 TeV. Our findings reveal how particle ratios change as the scale of the collision increases from the smallest to the largest. This includes an examination of strange and light hadrons produced in each type of interaction. This work not only confirms previous observations but also makes several new discoveries in this field.

We investigate the double parton distribution (DPD) $d\hat{\sigma}/d\hat{t}\otimes d\sigma$ and its associated fragmentation functions, in comparison to single parton distribution functions. Our study centers on calculating DPDs for various double parton combination processes, such as $pp \to pp\gamma\gamma$ and $pp \to pp\gamma Z$, within the framework of perturbative QCD at next-to-next-to-leading order. Additionally, the work involves proposing a technique for resolving contributions by different parton combinations in experimental measurements.

The behavior of Martian and Lunar regolith materials when subjected to mechanical deformation, particularly their viscoelastic properties, has not been extensively investigated. Researchers now have a unique opportunity to utilize these materials in the construction and manufacturing of space-based facilities. To better understand the rheological characteristics of these materials, a dynamic mechanical analyzer was employed to study their behavior under varying frequencies and temperatures. This allowed for a comprehensive examination of their viscoelastic properties in terms of storage and loss moduli. These findings can inform models of rheological behavior, thereby enabling improved predictions for engineering applications on the Martian and Lunar surfaces. Additionally, characterizing the viscoelastic properties of these materials may also open up new possibilities for their utilization in the construction of space-based facilities.

When a liquid film on a surface of a fibrous material loses adhesion to the surface due to weakening molecular interactions, the film breaks apart into distinct drops that move along the surface. This process occurs in both natural environments, such as the dissolution of water in plant leaves, and controlled laboratory settings, such as fluids within porous membranes. Despite the drop-formation phenomenon being observed for over a century, in fluids within porous materials, the underlying physical processes remain poorly understood. In this study, different theoretical models are developed to describe the flow of fluids through porous materials by accounting for the loss of adhesion between the fluid and the material's surface. These models, which rely on established fluid dynamics and surface physics, include one that simply considers the loss of adhesion, and another that takes into account the force holding the fluid to the surface. The models are applied to a single hair on a surface and the results are verified by comparing them to previously published data. The models also predict the size and movement of the drops, and the rate at which they form. This study provides an understanding of the drop-formation phenomenon and the role of surface interactions in fluids within porous materials.

We utilize data from 37 galaxies to examine the correlation between star formation rates calculated using the Prospector stellar evolution framework and observed properties. The analysis incorporates a range of indicators, including star formation rates based on different methods and properties such as galaxy color, metallicity, and velocity dispersion. We discovered that the accuracy of star formation rates derived from Prospector is closely linked to the available observational constraints. Furthermore, we find that incorporating far-ultraviolet luminosity helps to refine the predicted star formation rates. Our study highlights the importance of including specific constraints when inferring stellar populations, as omitting certain data can result in incorrect costraints on the star formation history. Additionally, we find that Prospector predicts similar rates using distinct, valid inputs, such as different types of star bursts, underscoring the need for further analysis to elucidate the history of star formation within galaxies.

We show that in any quadratic category, there exists an intrinsic, implicit definition of derivative that aligns with classical interpretation when the category is an algebraic orbifold. Building on this, we explore the concept of braided derivatives. In certain cases, such as in the case of linear and holomorphic eigenvalues, a general quadratic category's derivative leads to an association with a unique geometric meaning. Furthermore, in the context of orbifolds, exceptional braided auto-equivalences have a direct implication on the 21-dimensional space of second derivatives on the orbifold, which suggests an implicit connection to the space of BPS states. Establishing the relationship between quadratic categories and 2-Dimensional Refinements of 4-Gaussian models, we discover that any quadratic category is associated with an equivalent category that contains a unique geometric interpretation of its derivative. Building on this, we define a correspondence between 21-dimensional space of second derivatives and the 21-dimensional space of 2-point correlation functions.

We've established that the solutions to the Fisher-KPP equation have a certain level of smoothness and are globally well-defined in any dimension higher than one. This conclusion is derived from investigating the largest eigenvalue of a specific random matrix, whose elements are either -1 or 1, with a probability of 1/2 each. This eigenvalue problem is essentially equivalent to examining the solutions to a particular parabolic equation that involve the original eigenvalue problem as a parameter. By leveraging the maximum principle and establishing certain estimates, we can determine the conditions under which these solutions are smooth. Applying this understanding to the heat equation and the Fisher-KPP equation allows us to conclude that their solutions have a certain level of smoothness in any dimension higher than one. Interestingly, this analysis also provides insight into the regularity of the solutions to the eigenvalue problem and the parabolic equation, which have a certain level of smoothness in any dimension higher than one, as well.

The 2021 UbiComp Challenge sought to identify specific interactions using wearable devices placed on different parts of the body. The specific actions to be detected were not specified in the data provided, which consisted of various movements, such as writing on a paper, operating a vaccine dispenser, navigating on a map, playing a guessing game, and consuming food. Our approach involved using sensor data to identify the activity of interest, which in this case was writing on paper. We achieved this by applying the Bag-of-Word algorithm to time series data and then selecting the most relevant features using a heuristic feature selection technique. We evaluated several classification distances, ultimately determining that the Dynamic Time Warping distance was the most effective in identifying the activity of interest. Our results revealed that the Body Mass Index of the participant did not significantly influence the dispenser use and map navigation accuracy, but did affect food consumption. We successfully detected the activity of interest with an accuracy of 80.57% using a K Nearest Neighbors classifier.

This paper introduces a novel, flexible approach to modeling duration in sequences. Unlike traditional methods that only consider a single distribution for all sequences or a single variable per sequence, this new model takes into account the dynamic change of durations across adjacent time steps, similar to how neural networks handle complex dependencies. It takes the form of a recurrent neural network where each unit corresponds to a specific mathematical operation, combining the advantages of recurrent neural networks and duration-awareness to effectively learn from duration information. The model can be trained using a forward approach, similar to forward algorithm, and provides a way to evaluate the probability of durations and decode optimal sequences. The model's performance is demonstrated on real-world data, showing improved Markov model performance when duration is highly variable and outperforming a strong baseline model, especially for longer durations.

Occupancy modeling has emerged as a powerful tool for ecological research, allowing researchers to estimate the probability of species presence at specific locations. By incorporating data from multiple detection methods, researchers can make more accurate predictions, enhance statistical power, and reduce costs. Bayesian frameworks offer an efficient way to analyze occupancy data, offering a versatile approach to address various research questions. Utilizing Bayesian methods enables researchers to leverage Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations to analyze data sets of any size, analyze correlated data, and make inferences without requiring intricate algebraic calculations. This tutorial provides a step-by-step guide to implementing a simple Bayesian occupancy model and extends the concept to more complex models, including those that analyze data from multiple sources and occupy the same space. The knowledge presented in this tutorial can be applied to a wide range of applications, including multiple detection methods and occupancy models that analyze data from survey blocks.

Skincare is a collaborative research effort with a dual focus: developing
an artificial intelligence-based diagnostic tool for dermatologists and general
practitioners, as well as creating an educational platform for skin disease
awareness and education. The diagnostic system, built with deep learning models
and user-friendly interfaces in mind, offers the capabilities of a dermatologist
to aid practitioners in the accurate diagnosis and treatment of skin conditions.
Additionally, the project encompasses a website and school program aimed at
raising public awareness about skin diseases and the importance of proper skin
care, featuring interactive features and easily understandable content for a
general audience.

We've developed a novel Gaussian Process regression model to describe the diversity among Type Ia supernovae by incorporating their brightness variations and redshifts into a single unified framework. The model employs an exponential covariance function and utilizes observational data to inform its parameters. A Laplace prior is applied to the residual variance to ensure it remains consistent across all data points. Additionally, we introduced a Laplace regularization term to cull any unnecessary predictors and encourage the remaining variables to work in tandem. The revised model displays improved performance over prior methodologies in predicting SN Ia and accurately reflects the underlying structure of the data. We've tested our new model using the SN Ia dataset from Hubble, with and without intrinsic brightness data, and have demonstrated that it outperforms prior methodologies in both scenarios. When applied to intrinsic brightness data, our new model yields predictions in line with the Lambda-CDM cosmological model.

Using data from radio observations, researchers discovered substantial outflows
of neutral gas leaving the Milky Way. To understand these outflows, the team
created a computer model simulating star formation in the galaxy to predict
outflows. The model revealed that the rate of mass ejected into space is
considerably greater than the amount of new stars being formed. Specifically, the
mass ejected annually is around 1.4 times the mass of the sun, while the rate
of new stars forming each year is about 0.06 times the mass of the sun. The model
also indicated that most of the ejected gas moves at speeds under 90 kilometers
per second, which matches observations. The model further predicted that these
outflows could provide the raw material needed for the formation of new stars in
neighboring galaxies.

The interaction between a turbulent plume and suspended particles has been the subject of in-depth experimental investigations. The focus has been on understanding the phenomenon of particle entrainment within the plume and its contribution to turbulence. The experiments revealed an unexpected increase in the rate of particle entrainment when the plume's buoyancy flux opposes that of the particles, pointing to a causal link between this process and the plume's asymmetric flow dynamics. The findings also uncovered a previously unobserved physical process, attributed to the interaction between the plume and the particles' characteristic timescales, leading to an increase in the rate of particle entrainment. The research provides a theoretical framework and offers potential avenues for further investigation.

We develop a hypergraph model that captures the spread of contagion between interconnected entities, where subgroups of various sizes transmitted information, diseases, or behaviors within their respective networks. This is an extension of the standard graph model, where only direct neighbors influence each other, to a more general framework that accounts for larger influencing groups. Our focus is on understanding the infection rate, or the minimum mean degree of the hypergraph, representing the average influence received by each entity, which depends on the size of the underlying network and the number of entities within it. Our approach to estimating the infection rate involves a dynamic process where time increments in steps, and at each time, new infections occur in entities that have already been informed. After presenting the fundamental properties of the infection rate, we establish an lower bound on its value, based on the minimum mean degree of the hypergraph, and prove that this bound can be achieved in specific network configurations. Furthermore, we investigate the rate of convergence to this lower bound and show that convergence takes place at different rates over various network transitions. Our numerical experiments also support our theoretical findings on the behavior of the infection rate.

A theoretical investigation focused on the magnetic properties of a
perpendicular ferromagnetic bilayer under compressive strain, comprising
materials with different spin-orbit coupling. The strain's impact on the
companion ferromagnetic layer causes a unique spin texture that remains
identical to the original material but rotates in the opposite direction.
The ground state breaks symmetry in three dimensions, exhibiting a
meron-like arrangement induced by strain. The spin current at the interface
is analyzed in response to strain, and various in-plane transport properties
are examined in relation to strain.

Stars that experience rapid rotation changes can generate internal magnetic fields through dynamic processes, particularly in the overlying convective layers. We have created three-dimensional simulations of these internal dynamos, focusing on stars that rotate slowly to moderately. The experiments revealed that in slowly rotating stars, magnetic fields accumulate over time and remain constant, whereas in more rapidly rotating stars, these fields fluctuate between zero and a maximum value. These maximum magnetic field strengths are directly linked to the star's rotational period. The findings suggest that internal dynamos can produce magnetic cycles only in stars that rotate at moderate speeds or faster. The simulations also showed that in slowly rotating stars, magnetic fields are confined to specific regions, typically poleward, and remain relatively weak, usually no more than 1 G. The internal dynamos have a significant impact on the star's surface magnetic field only when the rotation period is under 15 days; elsewhere, surface magnetic fields are dominated by tidal forces, produced when a star, experiencing tidal heating, is in a binary system.

This paper introduces a dual learning model for complex, interactive tasks that integrate multiple inputs and outputs. We develop a network architecture that can function as both an autoencoder and a predictive model, utilizing shared encoding and decoding layers in an alternating mode. To enhance performance, a de-biasing technique is applied to minimize performance disparities between different input/output pairs. Experimental results on real-world data sets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed model and associated methods.

A new multi-threaded model checker called McMini has been developed, offering
high-speed model checking operations for concurrent systems implemented using
Pthreads. This advanced model checker leverages the features of the McSpi open
source library from University College London for efficient state manipulation.
Featuring a McMini core with McSpi's high-level functional programming capabilities
as well as optimized low-level C implementation, this tool provides improved speed
and efficiency over traditional model checking approaches. The McMini model
checker's performance has been demonstrated through comprehensive testing of seven
Pthreads-based benchmark suites, achieving remarkable speedup factors of up to
67x compared to the nearest competitor.

WhasApp is the most widely-used messaging app, with over two billion users worldwide, who send more than 65 billion messages daily. While its users trust the platform for personal and social communications, WhatsApp has faced criticism for allowing the spread of misinformation. In response, WhatsApp has introduced several features to address this issue, including a "forward mark," fact-checking partnerships, and educational campaigns. However, more needs to be done to combat the problem. Our research aims to understand the scale of misinformation spread on WhatsApp in Germany, using a quantitative approach, by analyzing media reports from 2018 to 2020. Our findings suggest that misinformation is presented in various forms, including structured and unstructured content, often accompanied by images, videos, or voice recordings. The next step is to investigate how users perceive the problem and what effective solutions look like.

A fixed population of individuals undergoes successive generations, 
wherein each individual is chosen at random to either reproduce or
retire. The process is governed by a utility function that maps
genotypes to non-negative real numbers. The structure of the population
evolves according to a mutational process, where each new generation's
genotypes are obtained by randomly altering the parent individuals' genotypes
via a specified mutation mechanism. Our study relies on a dictionary of
functions to encode the population's genetic state and utilizes a function
value on the Borel sigma-algebra to define a probability measure.
The resulting Markov chain is analyzed to derive necessary and sufficient
conditions for the asymptotic extinction of certain genotypes and a
characterization of the long-term genome distribution in the population.

To enhance the effectiveness of spoofing countermeasures, we introduce a novel feature design which utilizes attention mechanisms to improve speech artifact detection. In our proposed method, convolutional neural networks with attention blocks (ConvAFAE) utilize a convolutional autoencoder architecture to generate key and proxy features, which are then combined using an attention mechanism to produce a single output feature that indicates the presence of spoofed speech. A subsequent classification layer utilizing Euclidean distance or cosine similarity is used to classify the output feature. We evaluated the proposed method on the third speaker validation challenge dataset and found it to surpass previous state-of-the-art results, with a 2% improvement in EER and a 4% improvement in FPR95%.

This article provides a comprehensive review of contemporary Supergravity. The review begins by examining the mathematical foundations of Supergravity, including its connection to theories of quantum gravity and methods for constructing low-energy effective theories. The review then delves into key applications of Supergravity, such as calculating particle properties and understanding the structure of extra dimensions. The article concludes with an exploration of the most forward research outcomes in the field.

We examine the degenerate down-conversion process happening within a silicon microdisk, specifically considering the reverse pump orientation scenario. The coherent properties of the generated photon pairs are studied through the analysis of second-order and third-order correlation functions under various pump orientations and angular configurations. Our research demonstrates that reversing the pump's propagation direction leads to a significant enhancement in the coherence properties and correlation functions of the photon pairs. Furthermore, we verify that the coherence properties are preserved when the photon pairs are collected over broad ranges and observe significant enhancements in the third-order correlation functions' values. Such advancements position silicon microdisks as promising candidates for the development of highly coherent source systems for quantum applications and the exploration of novel fundamental phenomena.

This research examines the thermal behavior of various silicon surfaces treated by etching. Contrary to common assumptions, these investigations demonstrate that etched silicon does not act as an ideal thermally semi-conductive boundary as commonly believed. Instead, the studies employ Fourier's heat conduction equation, considering non-linear heat conduction in combination with capillary-driven flow, to analyze heat conduction within the solid phase and cross-boundary heat transfer. Specifically, the concentration of charge carriers near etched silicon surfaces differs significantly from that of buffer oxide etched silicon. Furthermore, the measurements in silicon reveal a higher thermal boundary conductance compared to buffer oxide etching. Nevertheless, the data show that this enhanced boundary conductance can be attributed to the presence of water and hydroxyl ions rather than the direct response of silicon itself. Lastly, the calculations suggest that even minor amounts of water at the silicon surface can exert a substantial influence on heat conduction.

We show that there is a significant difference in cardinality between sets that can be partitioned into Borel sets and those that can be partitioned into closed sets on the real line. This contrasts with a previous finding by Matthew Baker that such sets have similar cardinalities in the context of random graphs.

This study offers a fresh perspective on the CTAs' drawdown risk by providing diversification benefits to traditional portfolios composed of the S&P 500 index. Our research reveals that, on average, CTA performance is more resilient during periods of market volatility and subsequent recoveries, thereby indicating potential strategic importance in times of market turmoil. Although some investors view CTAs as a source of risk, our findings suggest that they could actually provide a valuable safety net for long-term portfolio managers who follow a traditional asset allocation plan. Our research employs multiple approaches to assess the CTA's value-added, including both subjective and objective methods, in order to counter potential biases associated with back testing. Our results remain consistent across these different methodologies and are further substantiated by examining the underlying trading strategies of specific CTA managers.

Evasion Evasion attacks are becoming increasingly common against various systems, including monitoring systems, which are used by law enforcement to detect encrypted communication protocols within network traffic. If successful, these attacks could allow illicit activities to go undetected, undermining efforts to detect and prevent crime. This could have serious consequences for those involved and the general public. In an effort to mitigate this, we have developed an assessment strategy to determine the effectiveness of counter-measures against evasion attacks. This is being accomplished by utilizing an evolving set of evasion attacks against a monitoring system, which is employed in a controlled online environment. Our current findings suggest that evasion attacks can evade more than 70% of law enforcement's monitoring systems, which could have significant implications for crime prevention and prosecution. It is worth noting that the details of these evasion attacks are subject to discretionary restrictions.

Magnetic films with a uniform in-plane magnetic field can support transverse magnon
propagation when a superconducting strip is deposited on its surface, cutting it into two
separate magnetic regions. The presence of these regions gives rise to new modes characterized
by magnons that are confined laterally and can travel long distances, exhibiting both reflective
and transmissive behavior. In the double-wavelength arrangement, where the two regions have nearly
equal width, the magnon propagation exhibits notable resonance behaviors, influenced by both
magnon frequency and strip width. Conversely, in the single-wavelength arrangement, where the two
regions have significantly different width, the magnon propagation exhibits a smooth, continuous
transition. The system's ability to support excitations at very low power levels holds great potential
for developing fast and efficient optical magnonic devices.

This study proposes a zero-shot federated learning framework that can handle novel data distributions without the need for model updates or communication between clients. The framework relies on metacognitive protocols to gather statistical information from each user and present it in a standardized form for universal model updating. To address distribution shifts, a semi-parametric framework is introduced, using only a limited number of unlabeled samples to learn a universal representation that differs from the initial one. The study introduces a new challenge problem, known as Class-IL, to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed method in adapting to unseen data distributions without requiring re-training. The results show that the proposed method successfully mitigates performance degradation caused by distribution shifts. Moreover, it offers a flexible and efficient solution to the federation-wide parameter alignment problem, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods by 10% and requiring significantly fewer communication steps than model aggregation based approaches.

The quantum Fourier transform, a crucial component of quantum computing and communication, particularly in high-dimensional multi-photon systems, faces significant challenges related to its practical implementation. These challenges stem from its inherent need to aggregate an enormous number of costly qubit rotations and massive numbers of highly correlated photons. Leveraging the concept of delayed measurement developed for multi-photon quantum computation, our innovative solution proposes a novel coherent measurement approach to overcome this challenge. By introducing a coherent gate-based implementation of the quantum Fourier transform, our design can achieve the necessary coherent shift, which was previously only demonstrated classically. Our research demonstrates that this coherent implementation can be combined with the existing entanglement-pulling technique to yield the desired photon scattering transformation, thereby making the quantum Fourier transform feasible for use in high-dimensional multi-photon quantum computing and communication.

This research focuses on the cascaded IRS-assisted MIMO system, where a multi-path channel connects the TX and RX through multiple IRS reflectors. Our proposed joint estimation technique uses optimization to determine the state of each IRS in conjunction with initial estimate adjustments, ultimately improving the accuracy of channel coefficient estimation. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in remaining robust to uncertainties in the system for a considerable number of trials.

The current study evaluates the effectiveness of carbon pricing policies in promoting local news reporting about public health issues, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. To investigate this, researchers utilized a unique dataset containing the advertising revenue of small newspapers in relation to their online coverage of COVID-19 stories. The analysis revealed significant variations in volume and content of local news coverage. To enhance understanding, the researchers subdivide the newspapers into three groups: those with sufficient advertising revenue to produce COVID-related content, those producing news without accompanying advertising, and those failing to address the crisis through their news content. The findings suggest that carbon pricing could potentially increase the number of news stories by 'price-sensitive' outlets, but only if such pricing directly affects their advertising revenue. Nonetheless, the most vulnerable news organizations face financial constraints, making it impractical for them to produce COVID-related news content, even if such pricing increases their advertising revenue. In a broader sense, the study underscores the importance of addressing the financial predicament of small news outlets in order to ensure diverse information sources. Furthermore, the research highlights the need to explore alternative sponsorship models that can support fact-based reporting on public health matters, including carbon pricing policies.

This investigation introduces an innovative technique for extrapolating neural network performance beyond its initial training scope, facilitated by counting. We also examine the underlying set-theoretic foundations of systematic counting, also known as quantification, which enables its application. This counting approach serves as a fundamental operation for constructing neural network classifiers and can be viewed as an iterative process of group-theoretic quotient formation. We showcase our methodology by analyzing the symmetric groups $S_n$ and $A_n$, for which the corresponding counting classifiers exhibit enhanced generalization capabilities. Notably, our analysis reveals instances where these classifiers yield $A_n$-invariant features, and in certain cases, these networks even surpass state-of-the-art challenge benchmarks established by Deep Neural Networks, including the challenging MNIST-SVHN and MNIST-M benchmarks.

Recent investigations into approximate set matching, as found in Bloom filters, have led to the introduction of xor filters, which offer reduced memory usage and faster matching times. This paper explores the performance of xor filters in relation to Bloom filters across a range of parameters. Through an examination of the distribution of hash outputs, we identify the optimal configuration for xor filters and demonstrate how their performance can be further optimized. Our analysis yields the following conclusions: (1) xor filters are a viable alternative to traditional Bloom filters for approximate set matching; (2) the optimal configuration for xor filters is when the hash outputs of two sets, A and B, are either entirely identical or differ in a small number of ways; and (3) the average number of differing hash outputs between A and B can be estimated using a simplified version of the Levenshtein distance. Based on these findings, we suggest an optimized hash function for xor filters and provide a detailed explanation of our results.

This article provides an overview of the Alexandrov body construction, its connection to divisorial Zariski decomposition, and its relationship to other geometric concepts such as the Zariski-Fletcher decomposition and the Shokry-Mella decomposition. It also introduces new geometric concepts and theorems, including the construction of a specific divisor on a non-big nef line bundle, associated closed subgroups of the algebraic Mori Dream Space, and the decomposition of the numerical dimension.

Our research focuses on uncovering hidden patterns in financial markets using advanced signal processing techniques, with a special emphasis on directional prediction. We believe that past price movements can be broken down into distinct frequency components, some of which harbor predictive power, much like how radio signals contain information across various frequencies. To reveal this, we use a sophisticated tool called the multivariate autoconvolution of past price data, which helps us identify the time frames that can predict future price directions. Our analysis, performed on one-minute British pound data from 2014 to 2018, yielded two significant time frequencies: one lasting 27.7 minutes and the other spanning 64.4 minutes. We found that the predictive power during the first 10 observations of each time period differs significantly, suggesting that the shorter time frame is more effective. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the British pound's volatility is higher when its price is increasing rather than decreasing, and this volatility indicator helps refine our directional predictions, increasing their accuracy.

This paper presents an unsupervised prototype clustering model called FLVoogd, which addresses two primary concerns: maintaining user privacy and preventing the inclusion of malicious data. FLVoogd achieves this through a two-phase approach where it first guesses user categories using pseudo-anonymized data and then refines those guesses with actual, securely encrypted data without revealing the initial estimates. As a consequence, FLVoogd prevents the model from being tricked by malicious actors providing fake data. Since pseudo-anonymized data is used in the initial phase, FLVoogd relies on an additional mechanism, which continuously monitors and updates the model to prevent it from being hacked in the same way. FLVoogd operates within existing Signal infrastructure and has successfully run real-world tests with 100,000 users, detecting and isolating suspicious users while protecting user data and preventing contamination from malicious data.

Recent advancements in sim2real transfer have shown significant potential, 
enabling direct use of simulated data to train autonomous vehicle models 
without the need for actual testing. While previous studies have focused on 
using simulated data in isolation, our work aims to explore the impact 
of combining sim2real transfer with real-world data, a approach we term 
sim2real+real. Our key finding is that using both simulated and real data 
results in better performance when compared to using either alone. To 
investigate this further, we employed a dataset with diverse scenes and 
formulated a new loss function to combine the two data sources. When 
applied to a range of advanced autonomous driving tasks, our approach 
not only surpassed the performance of traditional methods but also provided 
more consistent results across different evaluation configurations.

Deepfakes have significantly improved in quality and reach, accessible to anyone through widely available creation software, yet raise serious concerns regarding their spreading influence. Although research on detecting deepfakes has accelerated in the last 5 years, the media's spread has already had significant societal and political impacts, suggesting the need for improved detection methods and distribution control. To address this, our research presents a novel framework integrating Neural Network-based image authentication with a decentralized blockchain, aiming to prevent and detect malicious media distribution. By utilizing a unique signature produced by the authentication process, the owner of the malicious media is held accountable and rewarded when the false media is officially acknowledged. Our proposed framework is now the first implementation of a decentralized deepfake detection and prevention system, evaluated using the FaceForwards dataset and MVTec 3D Industrial dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting known and novel manipulations and providing an automatic and fair compensation mechanism for victims of false media spread.

The diversity in sizes of temperate planets leads to a variety of atmospheric settings, ranging from massive to thin ones, with differing characteristics in terms of gas compositions, pressures, and temperature gradients. This study employs theoretical models to explore the atmospheres of small and large temperate planets, with special focus on those similar in size to TRAPPIST-1 b and K2-25 b. Given the limited understanding of gas exchange processes in small atmospheres, this research utilizes clip model simulations to investigate the carbon-nitrogen chemistry in these planets. We find that massive atmospheres on small planets are rich in nitrogen and have reduced carbon levels, whereas the opposite is true for large-planet atmospheres with lower nitrogen and carbon levels. These patterns are consistent with primary and secondary interactions between carbon and nitrogen gases. Implications of these findings may be seen four years following the publication of the model constraints, specifically in terms of atmospheric retention efforts. Future studies should prioritize direct gas composition readings in small- and large-planet atmospheres to validate these theoretical findings.

A significant breakthrough in modeling neural dynamics was achieved with the introduction of the Hopfield network, a McCulloch-Pitts network that allowed for a vast number of states while exhibiting attractors. However, this model fell short in its ability to effectively learn patterns. To improve upon this design, researchers added an training algorithm, a backpropagation method based on a local and global reward, to the network. This upgraded model, the McCulloch-Pitts network with a local and global reward, can be viewed as a specific instance of the counterfactual gradient Thompson sampling algorithm. After applying an efficient desynchronization method, the network's ability to effectively learn capabilities was realized. In contrast to the classic Hopfield network, this model was capable of learning tasks that required fine-grained differentiation.

The outstanding performance achieved by OCR systems for out-of-vocabulary words in scene text recognition models heavily relies on the accuracy and comprehensess of the training dataset. Currently, the widely-used ICDAR 2013 dataset is the source of the largest public OCR dataset and is the standard reference point for evaluating scene text recognition models. However, due to its limitations in complexity and diversity of textual information, it is not suitable for assessing the capabilities of the most advanced deep learning algorithms. In contrast, the recently released SVTT dataset, comprising a significant collection of out-of-vocabulary words not present in the ICDAR 2013 dataset, presents an opportunity for enhancing the accuracy of current state-of-the-art models and exploring novel approaches to scene text recognition. In this study, we draw inspiration from the recent successes of Automatic Speech Recognition, proposing a two-stage approach that utilizes the ICDAR 2013 dataset for model pre-training and the SVTT dataset for training the models to recognize out-of-vocabulary words. In addition to the proposed approach, we also compile an extensive dataset, OutOfVoc_SRTR, comprising approximately 300K words, 2.8 million characters, and 18.4K word tokens, in addition to existing datasets, to provide a comprehensive evaluation benchmark for scene text recognition models. In accordance with the standards of the state-of-the-art model for out-of-vocabulary words, we assess the efficacy of this approach using the proposed OutOfVoc_S

We present an approach that leverages validated numerics to accurately calculate isolated branches of solutions in parameter-dependent problem sets, $d(x,u)=0$, where $x$ and $u$ are vectors and parameters, respectively.
